speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I should like to comment on certain aspects of the budget concerning industrial development.
Of course, I do not want to repeat the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on the state of the Canadian economy, except to mention again that our exports are faring relatively well, with a surplus trade balance estimated, on an annual basis, at $2.75 billion, which helps to give us, for the first time since 1952, a surplus in our balance of payments. I note that this results partly from the success of the government's fight against price increases, and I also note that it is taking place in spite of the inevitable re-evaluation of the Canadian dollar.
I also note that the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, comments on the slowing down of the rate of economic growth this year, estimated at 2.5 or 3 per cent for 1970, compared to 5 per cent in 1970. Although the rate of growth is now improving, the government, in view of persistent unemployment, has decided to give it an extra push by initiating additional incentives.
The government, as we know, faced two alternatives. The first consisted of general measures such as tax reductions, which the government felt could lead to a return of galloping inflation. The other alternative was adoption of specific, selective measures, geared to specific regions, specific industries and specific individuals. As we know, it has chosen the second alternative. Had the government chosen the first one, the opposition would of course have accused it of lacking intelligence, finesse and subtlety. Had it chosen them both, the opposition might have accused it of irresponsibility. But as it has chosen the first one, it is accused of lacking courage.
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the government will never win that game, because there always will be criticism.
But by choosing the first alternative, that is selectivity, the government is in good company. In a recent OECD commentary, for instance, a Committee on economic policy stated, and I quote:

-'in cases where unemployment is rising towards unacceptable levels, attention should be directed to the possibility of selected action directed to areas of high unemployment, rather than indiscriminate increases in public expenditure or general tax cuts.'
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

Thus we are in good company when we choose a selective approach rather than a general one.
As regards industrial development, Mr. Speaker, there are, in the budget of the Minister of Finance, four measures which for me, as Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, have a tremendous value, and I know that hon. members will want to keep them in mind too.
These four measures proceed from a concern for reinforcing the industrial base, and this shows that the short term concern meets the long term one. Here they are: (1) The expansion of the industrial incentive program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is already well known. (2) Additional capital cost allowances to manufacturers and processing industries which may result in a tax abatement amounting up to $25 million, and bring to Canada a possible $3 million investment. (3) Measures providing for loan insurance and direct loans to some especially affected industrial sectors; (4) Subsidies to the shipbuilding industry.
Obviously, I would like to discuss the last two items. First of all, why is this assistance provided to those industries, more specifically to the footwear industry which has come up to join the textile and clothing industries? Why this assistance to shipbuilders?
The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) has pointed out in a recent speech-and this, by the way, happens to be the only positive things he said then-that there was a relationship between the demands arising out of international trade liberalization and the demands of industrial efficiency.
In other words, if we, the people of Canada, strive to trumpet forth the advantages of free international trade

December 8, 1970

and make it pay, then the Canadian industry must become highly competitive. Otherwise, our philosophy does not agree with our interests. And this is my concern at this time.
Exports are faring relatively well, especially in the primary and semi-manufactured products sectors. We are selling easily enough our grain, our oil, our gas, our coal and our materials to international markets.
But what about manufactured products? Obviously that sector is making progress, but it is encountering difficulties and will always have them because international competition is and will remain extremely keen.
However, Mr. Speaker, it should be mentioned that we are progressing. Ten years ago, our exports accounted for approximately 10 per cent of manufactured products. Today, they represent between 35 and 40 per cent.
I agree that cars play a most important role. In any event, we have progressed, but may I reiterate that competition is fierce, particularly under the current circumstances of international trade which are lower tariffs, frequently involving protectionist threats, especially in Canada, a reduction in the national defense budget, a most healthy dollar and in certain industrial sectors, a desire by Canadian workers to attain wage parity with their American counterparts.
Is it not self-evident, Mr. Speaker, that we must give this sector of secondary industries, where the best prospects for creating jobs are, all the consideration that the circumstances I have just described warrant?
So we must continuously try to rationalize our manufacturing sector, and in this respect, all the tools available to the government and the public sector must be used.
I shall not mention all those available to my department as well as to some others, but this budget contains a provision which seems of particular interest to me- the extension of the General Adjustment Assistance Program to the footwear industry. You will recall that this extension had already been made to the textile and clothing industries.
This decision, I think, deserves some specific attention from hon. members.
In most cases, Mr. Speaker, this rationalization process is ensured by industry itself. There are also cases where it is not done, unfortunately, especially when industrial sectors are endangered and become vulnerable because of the liberal trade policy of the federal government. Where profits are lower and the future looks less promising, I feel that the government may and must contribute, in short may and must try to help private enterprise to rationalize and modernize its operations, or just to keep up to date as is often the case.
Mr. Speaker, we know that there is a program of manpower conversion to which the federal government contributes some $300 million a year. I think it is normal that a few millions of dollars be contributed also yearly to ensure that the conversion of industry itself, of
The Budget-Mr. Pepin
factories, takes place where there are particular problems of the type that I have outlined.

The general assistance program is known to many members of the House, but possibly not well enough. I wish to spend five minutes to describe it.
The GAAP program was established in 1968 to provide financial and technical support to Canadian manufacturers to take advantage of export opportunities arising out of the Kennedy round tariff cuts made by Canada and other countries. That is the main purpose of it.
The program is administered by a general adjustment assistance board which consists of a chairman and two members from the business community, as well as members from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It will soon include members of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to ensure that maximum co-ordination is accomplished.
The Board is authorized to provide three forms of assistance. The first form is government assistance of up to 90 per cent of loans made by private lenders to manufacturers for the restructuring of their operations. This is a loan. There is a charge of one per cent of the sum involved. The second form is direct government loans to manufacturers who have been seriously injured or threatened with serious injury and are unable to obtain an insured loan. In some cases then there is the possibility of a direct government loan.
The third form is grants of up to 50 per cent of the cost of services of qualified consultants required for the developments of sound restructuring proposals.
To date, the board has authorized loan insurance of $32.6 million to assist 30 manufacturers. No manufacturers have qualified for direct loans. Grants totalling $77,000 have been approved for consulting assistance for 10 manufacturers. I wish to give some examples to illustrate how useful the program has been.
A small Ontario based appliance manufacturer had been showing outstanding growth in sales and earnings. Exports sales in particular increased from $105,000 in 1968 to $700,000 in 1969 as a result of an aggressive sales policy combined with the Kennedy round tariff reductions. Further growth was limited because of the unavailability of funds to finance the required inventory buildup. The GAAP board authorized insurance of a $300,000 working capital loan early this year. With this financing, exports for 1970 will reach $1.4 million. Further, outstanding growth is projected for 1971.
Another example is a Maritime manufacturer who had developed a product line which was well received in the United States Market. The Kennedy round reductions further improved the market potential, but sales increases were restricted by limited plant capacity and inadequate inventory financing. The GAAP program provided a grant to finance a portion of the cost of a consulting study which recommended changes in plant

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Pepin
layout to streamline production flows and more than double plant capacity. The board later authorized insurance of a $470,000 loan to enable the company to implement the consultant's recommendation and provide inventory financing. The combination of grant and insured loan assistance will enable the company to increase export sales by $1.3 million per year by 1972.
It is forecast that as a result of the loan insurance authorized to date, exports in 1971 will be $28 million higher than they would have been without GAAP. For 1972 and 1973 the equivalent figures are $54 million and $89 million. I suggest that this is a very valuable program, Mr. Speaker. Now, if the program is good for exports, why should it not also be good for the domestic market? Extension of the program for that purpose was announced a few weeks ago in respect of textiles and clothing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announced the other night that it would be extended now to the footwear industry. I do not think anyone will disagree with that. I hope not. Parliamentary approval is now being sought through supplementary estimates for extensions of GAAT to all three sections: textiles, clothing and footwear. By so doing, we shall be contributing to the process of rationalization of those industries.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I might add that a further amendment to the GAAP program will authorize the board to insure loans made to certain non-manufacturing firms providing financial, marketing or other services essential for the operations of eligible manufacturers.
The situation is this, Mr. Speaker. A manufacturing plant somewhere in Stormont, let us say, would be in a better position if somebody was taking responsibility for financing, warehousing, marketing, or the like. The GAAP program, which up to now, could be used only by manufacturers, will now be offered to those who contribute indirectly to manufacturing. Again, I believe this is a good move. May I underline the importance of the announcement made the other day by the Minister of Finance with respect to the extension of the GAAP program to the footwear industry.

The footwear industry, as we know, is very important in Canada because it provides employment to 20,000 or
30,000	workers. However, being so fragmented, it is now going through a difficult period of adjustment. It is also submitted to strong pressures from imports.
I have here some figures that I would like to quote: [English]
Fifteen footwear firms in Canada have gone out of business in the past 12 months. In the first half of 1970, the volume of imported leather footwear was some 16 per cent higher than in the first half of last year and this trend is expected to continue. Six of the larger firms, employing about 2,600 workers, have recently requested federal government assistance in restructuring their operations to enable them to compete effectively. The import pressure is great, and this pressure comes not only
'Mr. Pepin.]
from low cost countries but from highly industrialized countries such as Italy, France, United Kingdom and the United States. The only real possibility in these circumstances is for the Canadian footwear industry, the leather section in particular, which still has 80 per cent of the domestic market, to become as efficient as possible. If they do so, not only will they keep that good large share of the domestic market but they will export a lot more than they are exporting today.
Everybody agrees with this. The Canadian footwear industry and the clothing industry possess originality, have ideas, and have style. They could produce for the Canadian market, and export a lot more than they do now.
Again, in order to do that, they need to be fully modernized; they need to specialize; they need to integrate. They agree with this estimate of their needs. They say, though, we should do something to help them do just that. And this is what is intended by the extension of the GAAP program.

The same concern for rationalization can be found in the government decision, as the result of increasing international demand, to assist the shipbuilding industry for export purposes. We know that this grant will range from 14 to 17 per cent, according to the tonnage of the ship.
The main purpose of that decision, confirmed by the Minister of Finance, is evidently to contribute to maintain a certain number of jobs. Jobs in that sector throughout Canada have decreased by some 5,000 since 1966 and they now number between 5,000 and 6,000. But if the steps already announced were not taken, perhaps 1,000 others would disappear during 1970 and next year. Consequently, it is essential to act.
In my statement of November 27 last, I emphasized the importance of reducing costs in this industry. It is easy to say. But the only way to do it is to try and produce more than one unit at a time, to build in small series. This is why both the number of ships being built and the budgetary measure encouraging exports are important.
I insisted also on the importance of diversification and specialization in order to lessen the vulnerability of shipyards in terms of fluctuations of the national and international demand.
Mr. Speaker, people should not believe that this desire for rationalization in the shipyard sector has only come up recently: my department has a Defence Material Industry Productivity Program known as DIP which has already tackled and made an important contribution to the problem. In fact, several shipyards, including St. John Shipbuilding, Marine Industries, Vickers, Davie Shipbuilding have already shared in the DIP program of my department to the amount of $3 million and have improved their production.
What about the result? I gave it in my release of the other day: "It is significant that a number of our yards
iv


December 8, 1970

are already producing efficiently a wide variety of heavy equipment such as pressure vessels, penstocks, gates, steel structures, industrial machinery and equipment and rail car, etc."
Do people know for instance that Marine Industries in Sorel and Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon are already devoting 50 per cent of their activities to projects other than shipbuilding?
That is an attempt to diversify which I thought worth mentioning.
In conclusion, making secondary industry more modern, diversified and specialized is one of the basic concerns of my department and of the government. I wanted to show today how the two measures announced by the Minister of Finance-the extension of the temporary assistance program and the subsidies to shipbuilding-were part of a larger framework, that of continuing improvement of Canada's industrial base, which will enable us to serve the domestic market more efficiently and to increase our exports.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question arising out of his remarks in connection with shipbuilding? It occurs to me that once the ships were built they might have foreign crews. Are further steps planned so that we might have not only more Canadian shipbuilding but more Canadians manning the ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is one of the many questions which was raised by the Robertson report, the possibility of having a Canadian merchant navy. The report is still being considered but, along with other studies, as I said on a previous occasion, no decision has been made on the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to comment in detail upon the remarks of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), though I have no doubt a number of my hon. friends will do so. At the outset of his observations, the hon. gentleman referred to his pleasure concerning the state of our exports. I should like to remind him, before I go any further, that the large balance of trade presently in our favour is perhaps due not so much to any increase in our exports as it is to a reduction in our imports. I also express the hope that the minister will not be so lost in admiration for the balance of trade this year that he will overlook some of the difficulties he and I discussed the other day in connection with future Canadian exports, particularly to Britain and the common market.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
With regard to the budget, this budget marks the end of a so-called period of restraint and the adoption by the government of some sort of goal of expansion. The government ends this period of restraint not with a full treasury but with a substantial and increasing budgetary
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
deficit. It ends this period of restraint with the country experiencing massive unemployment, with its antiinflationary program in ruins, indeed dismantled, and with the Prices and Incomes Commission retiring into a period of seclusion.
Despite this, the minister told us the other night that everything is going to be great. Unfortunately, the minister has not yet been right. Let us consider just how wrong he has been. I am not going to go back to 1968, when he told us that we were going to have a balanced budget and, in fact, we had a deficit of $750 million. There is no need to go back to 1968, let us consider 1970.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about 1969?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will be happy to talk to the minister about 1969 at any other time but let me talk about 1970 at the moment. Let us go back to the March budget when the minister took a good, clear look forward. One thing he said was that the situation was such that '"we need to consider introducing consumer credit controls to keep the economy from running away on us". He predicted a surplus of $250 million for the year. During the first few months he abandoned any idea of introducing consumer credit controls, and by October he was talking about a budgetary deficit of $150 million. In his budget speech the other night, he talked about a budgetary deficit of $350 million.
The minister refers to this as "a process of constant and continuing review". That is how he describes it. What we really have on the part of the minister is a constant and continuing effort to adjust to his previous errors in estimates, his previous forecasting mistakes. First of all, the minister realizes that he is completely wrong about consumer credit regulations. Then, he realizes things are not going the way he calculated so he increases some sharing arrangements made with the provinces to "reverse the process", as he called it. Then, as the year went on he realized that he and his colleagues had created a virtual catastrophe in the housing program, and he now sees the need to put more money into the program.
We now have this budget. From March until today, there has been a constant effort on the part of the minister to readjust to the very serious errors in forecasting he made last march. The forecasts of the March budget were a complete botch. No one need take my word for that; all he need do is to follow the manoeuvring of the minister ever since. At first, he was rather cautious and very complacent, but his manoeuvres escalated until recently they reached a flurry of activity as the extent of unemployment in this country finally became apparent, apparent even to this government with its superb talent for seeing only what it wants to see and absolutely nothing else.
The minister said on television the other night in a program called "Encounter" that his forecasting this year had been pretty good, that things had worked out just about as he had anticipated. That, Mr. Speaker, is patent-

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
ly untrue in view of the manoeuvring and scrambling that he has been doing ever since he made those forecasts. I must say I find it impossible to believe that the government foresaw what has happened but sat back and allowed it to happen. I am prepared to believe that the government is incompetent, but I am not prepared to believe that it foresaw the present levels of unemployment, for example in the province of Quebec, British Columbia and the Atlantic provinces. I am not prepared to believe that the minister and his colleagues foresaw this level of unemployment and accepted it, despite the hard boiled remarks made by his Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding the degree of unemployment that he is prepared to accept. I can see that the government is absurdly complacent, but I do not believe it is that cruel.
One of the most alarming aspects about the whole economic scene in Canada today is that, despite these terrific errors in forecasting and judgment, the Minister of Finance still believes that his forecasting was good. His capacity for self-delusion almost goes beyond the degree of complacency that the government exhibits.
The budget of March was a bad mistake in judgment. The slowdown in our economy had already been allowed to go too far. There were warnings from the Economic Council of Canada and from others. To continue deliberately to run down the economy below par, and deliberately to hold down the growth in the economy below the rate of growth of the labour force, with the consequent increase in unemployment, is inexcusable. Why did the government make such a distorted judgment of the outlook last year? Was it to show those fellows in the organized labour movement just who is boss in this country? It was said to be done in the name of fighting inflation. I have said many times that the minister's policy was inhumane.
The minister and his friends are fond of talking about OECD. Massive unemployment is not accepted by OECD as a weapon or tool for fighting inflation. It is not accepted because it weakens the will to fight inflation. Despite all the talk about OECD by my hon. friend opposite, no government in western Europe would accept anything like the degree of unemployment that this government has accepted during the past year.
Furthermore, there is not the slightest evidence that unemployment to this degree is in any way a necessary part of an effective fight against inflation in this country. I admit that when a government brings on a recession and creates massive unemployment, certainly the rate of price increases will slow down. But the Canadian people have had to pay a very heavy price. Not only have they had to pay a very heavy price, but the government has not dealt with the basic causes of inflation in this country. The government has not established any defence against the development of inflation in future in this country. Indeed, the anti-inflationary machinery of this government lies in ruins. The Prices and Incomes Commission has reverted to the status of a study group and, as it has done so, it has made this pronouncement: The Prices and Incomes Commission has said that unless
there is moderation in wage demands in this country we can expect either excessive inflation, excessive unemployment or compulsory prices and wage controls. That is the pronouncement of the Prices and Incomes Commission on its way to retiring into obscurity. It is a grim prospect, in addition to the existing unemployment and other difficulties of this country.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Prices and Incomes Commission also accepts and emphasizes the view that fiscal and monetary policies are not by themselves adequate tools to fend off inflation. This is also the view of the OECD, and it is not for the Minister of Finance or anybody else to pretend that they are adequate in themselves.
Here we have massive unemployment and we have a big budgetary deficit. We have a government which has no idea how it is going to cope with inflation when we do achieve something like full employment again, short of the prospect of compulsory control. The minister says that the main weapons against inflation must be monetary and fiscal policies. He says voluntary restraints can work only for a short time. Let me say two things to him, sir. Monetary and fiscal policies will not do the job by themselves and even compulsory controls can work only for a short time.
I admit that no country has worked out a satisfactory program in respect of a voluntary income restraint policy. I admit that, but nevertheless nearly every country now recognizes the need, as does the OECD. The government has become aware I think that voluntary restraints must be based on co-operation, and cannot be imposed by a government or government agency. Such a policy has a much better chance of getting started and working if it is introduced in a period when inflationary pressures are not too great.
The government tried to introduce such a policy from above, and tried to do it when inflationary pressures were very great. I had urged an approach to this sort of thing in this House as far back as 1967. The government delayed, and when it tried it failed to get co-operation. As a result, the effort was abandoned. I say in all sincerity that if inflationary pressures have now ceased, and if the rate of inflation has now decreased, this is the time the government should be trying rather than giving up. It should be redoubling its efforts to participate with management and labour in working out a program of restraints.
I do not say this is easy but I say the government should try. I also suggest that tax reductions at this time would have helped create an appropriate climate for this kind of initiative in this country. If the government was able, in a period lacking strong inflationary pressures, to work out a framework of restraint on the basis of cooperation, then fiscal and monetary policies could be used to prevent an over-heating and building-up of excessive pressure. Then, we would have a chance in Canada of attaining satisfactory employment and stability at the same time. Instead, the government has thrown in the towel. Its boast of success against inflation is not the

December 8, 1970

result of superior management but simply the result of a severe slowdown of our economy and severe unemployment in our country. Now, we have a slowdown and unemployment, and the outlook is for more inflation as our economy expands because this government clearly knows no way to head off inflation. Indeed, the government is already commencing to increase its own pressures on the capital markets of this country.
The keynote of this budget, if there is one, is expansion. What is the government doing with regard to unemployment and what is its approach? Its approach is basically one of pump priming concentrated in areas of slow growth in the country. The reason given for increasing expenditures and loans rather than reducing taxes is that this is an effort to pin-point where the expansion is to take place in order to benefit areas of slow growth.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said this afternoon that the government cannot resort to a reduction in taxation without producing galloping inflation. With all respect to him, there is nothing to back up his statement. In fact, there is very good reason to believe that a reduction in income tax at this time would modify wage increases. In any event, there is not the slightest reason to believe that a reduction in income tax at this time would lead to galloping inflation in this country.
When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce purported to justify the resort to increased expenditures in certain areas rather than reducing taxes he again quoted the OECD as advising countries to consider selective approaches to unemployment rather than such general measures as reduction in taxation. That advice of the OECD makes very good sense for countries in western Europe, for example. It makes excellent sense for a government that has virtually full employment, except in certain areas of the country.
I suggest it is nonsense on the part of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to take this advice which makes very good sense under other conditions and apply it to Canada where there is massive unemployment across the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I say that my program will combine both.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, sir. I anticipate there is a much more fundamental reason for the government choosing the course it did rather than choosing to reduce taxation. I think it is because of its mechanistic view of the economy of Canada. It believes you can slow down the economy any time by tightening the screws, and obviously you can. Conversely, the government seems to believe that you can bring about expansion when and where you will simply by loosening the screws and putting more gas into the machine by spending more money. Certainly, you can slow down the economy that way but you cannot necessarily assume this is a machine that you can start up again simply by feeding it a little more gas. The economy is not just a piece of machinery which the government can regulate in this way.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
The expectations and confidence of individuals play a great role. The minister, in his budget speech, stated his expectations but he certainly did not create confidence. He did not carry a conviction to this country that his projections were going to prove to be true. It is fair to say that everyone in this country was virtually shaken by the increase in taxation and by the increase in taxation I mean the imposition of the surtax beyond the time when it was clearly understood it was to be discontinued. I think everybody in the country is disconcerted by the implications of this move by the minister. I say there ought to have been a tax decrease, particularly for people with lower incomes. The Minister of Finance admitted that a tax decrease would have an expansionary effect on the economy.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I say, too, it would provide a great psychological lift. Indeed, such a reduction in taxation leading to an expansion in the economy would tend to generate more revenue for the government. The government, therefore, would not be giving up very much revenue as a result of reducing taxation in a way which would lead to expansion of the economy. The government did not choose to do that. It chose instead to maintain taxation, and then some. It chose this course because I believe the government thought it was better for the government to raise and spend money in order to try to pinpoint where growth will take place than it was for the government to free the individual when this was possible. I say this attitude of the government toward increased taxation is depressing and is counterproductive. Such an attitude certainly adds to the uncertainties that are around as a result of the floating dollar and adds to the uncertainties that are around as a result of the failure of the Minister of Finance to clarify what he proposes to do in respect of tax reform and what recommendations of the committee he proposes to accept.
All this uncertainty is holding up decisions in the private sector of the economy. As I have said, this action of the government in increasing taxation when it ought to be reducing taxation adds to the uncertainties. I might be more accurate if I were to say this decision by the Minister of Finance to increase taxation at this time gives certainty to the fears of many Canadians that the minister will use tax reform, as he is now using economic disparity, as an excuse or a disguise for higher taxation in this country. That is a pretty depressing prospect. The driving force of the economy is not just the money the government pumps around in this country. Certainly, intelligent fiscal policy is an important factor in growth and stability. But individual motivation is important, incentive is important and confidence is important. The government is destroying incentive, is destroying confidence and is discouraging the people of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Over the years we have heard a lot about the fight against poverty. The minister referred to

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
old age security and pensions. The other night he said we are increasing these pensions and the assistance to the aged just at the right time. The right time for whom? The right time for the pensioners was a couple of years ago. Yet so much does the minister identify the interests of the government with the interests of the older people of this country that he assumes this is just the right time for the older people of the country. He asks them to wait until next spring for this kind of help. The minister says it is just the right time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For the economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For the economy, I see. I am sorry but I am no more ready now than I was before to accept the minister's judgment concerning what is just the right time for the economy, either. It may be more obvious that the minister's timing was not in the interests of the older people of the country, but one does not have to look much further to decide it was not right for the economy, either.
Certainly, the government is not attacking poverty. Certainly, there is no sign in the government's white paper on social security that the government intends to attack poverty. I want to say that a buoyant economy in this country is essential to any attack on poverty. First of all, a buoyant economy is necessary in order to reduce unemployment which has added so much to the poverty in this country in the last year or so and, second, a buoyant economy is necessary to produce the revenue needed for an effective high productivity program. I say that the prompt stimulation of our economy is an essential part of the fight against poverty in Canada today. The same applies to regional disparity and regional poverty. Surely, it is not necessary for me to emphasize the importance I attach to the fight on regional disparity. It is not necessary for me to emphasize the importance I attach to moving ahead more rapidly in areas of slow growth in this country. I believe this government will get nowhere in an effort to help these areas of slow growth unless the economy of the country generally is buoyant.
The areas of slow growth, such as the Atlantic Provinces, parts of Quebec and parts of the other provinces, are the first to feel the effect of any slackness in the national economy. It is in these areas the slackness tends to concentrate. More than ten years ago, this fact was emphasized to the governments of the Atlantic provinces by consultants we used. Professor Alex Cairncross, who later became the chief Economic Advisor to the government of Great Britain, emphasized to us that the Atlantic provinces and other areas of slow growth certainly needed development programs but that these would do little good in those areas unless the national economy was healthy and going forward at the same time. I have been saying this for years. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) apparently finally has realized this also because he said so in the House the other day. This realization, however, certainly is not reflected in the government's policy as announced in the budget. As one would anticipate, the national slowdown in our economy has created new depressed areas.

If the Minister of Finance continues in the same way, the whole country will require designation pretty soon. Indeed, in the sense that the whole economy is below par, it almost requires this today. If the economy picks up substantially, such programs could help Quebec and other areas of slow growth-although I must say that the concept of designation is coming pretty close to being absurd, if it is not there already, when one considers the proportion of the country that has now been designated. I repeat that I am certainly in favour of such measures of help. But the best immediate help to the Province of Quebec, the Atlantic provinces and other areas of slow growth would be a rapid increase in national prosperity. This is the measure that would afford the most immediate help to all these regions because these are the regions which feel the greatest impact of the national recession that is taking place. I say that tax reduction is the most immediate and effective way to produce this prompt stimulation of our economy. Such a tax reduction could be associated with specific measures of encouragement.
Tax reduction would create the psychological climate required for expansion, as the Minister of Finance admits. This was the course which should have been taken, rather than the choice made by the Minister of Finance which was a tax increase, with an all-wise government increasing its encouragement in certain sectors of the economy and just assuming that its increased expenditures as well as some kind of an expanding monetary supply in themselves would ensure an expanding national economy, without which the minister's help to slow growth areas will accomplish very little or practically nothing.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Of course, I suppose it is possible that the minister may be right for once in this projection, but what a chance to take. If the economy is slow to respond, after being screwed down the way it has and worried after this budget, consider first of all the beautiful fiscal mess that the minister will have created both for himself and for his provincial counterparts. But, more important, think of the disillusionment and the bitterness that will have been created among our youth and among the hard core unemployed.
Our economy is not just a machine. The minister and his colleagues talk in terms of inputs and outputs, but what he is really dealing with is people. He is fooling around with the lives of people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know his job is difficult. I do not think he is an unkind man. I assume he is a man with some feeling and he probably says to himself when one of his policies creates some unemployment that it hurts him more than it hurts the unemployed, rather like the parent taking the whip and beating the child. I say to the minister in all sincerity that his methods of forecasting are not reliable enough to justify the kind of decision he has taken in his budget. In fighting inflation he resorts to overkill-unintentionally I am sure, because he did not
December 8, 1970

know what he was doing-and in fighting unemployment in Canada today he is guilty of underkill. I say the economy needs a large stimulus now, and despite what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said, this would not be stoking the fires of future inflation. A cut in taxes now would not stoke the fires of future inflation. There are all kinds of slack in the economy today, and a large stimulus now need not be a continuing stimulus. As the economy picked up, the minister could start applying the braking process. But what he needs to ensure now is that the economy picks up, and he should not just take that for granted.
I say to the minister that his forecasting methods are crude, that the government's methods of manipulating the economy are crude, and that the economy is far more complex than he and his advisors conceive, otherwise they would never have concocted the white paper on tax reform. Instead of a tax reform designed to fit our economy, the government has been trying to fit the economy to its concept of tax reform. Now, instead of producing a budget designed to suit the needs of this country, a living, breathing complex of relationships among people, the government chooses to treat the economy as a piece of machinery which it can adjust at will, as if it were a question of putting in a little gas in the right place and in the right amounts. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, don't you believe him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hundreds of thousands of Canadians are already paying a high price in unemployment. The budget does virtually nothing for them in the coming months, and they will continue for months to pay for the government's past mistakes. I ask, how long are we all going to have to pay for the present mistakes of the government in the budget that we are now discussing? One newspaper describes this budget as "a scattergun approach". That is certainly not being too hard on the government. Apparently the government has decided that such an approach is sufficient, because it still does not really believe our economy is in trouble. In fact, after reading the budget speech itself, one would think that there are no real problems in Canada at all. In language consistent with the language in the Speech from the Throne, this budget speech once again takes a complacent, unconcerned line that has become the hallmark of this government. It talks smugly about "improving trends", tells us that we are "moving out of the pause", and generally simply takes for granted what it should be proving.
This budget is really little more than a gesture, a sort of public relations gimmick, a pat on the head of the unemployed and the Canadian people to say "there, there, you will see; everything will be all right". It is a little like a mother saying she will kiss away the hurt suffered by her little child when he has a fall. That is O.K. if it is just a scratch, but the government's policies have wounded our economy far more deeply than that. I say it is an insult for this government to suggest that
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
now all it has to do is to kiss away our wounds. It is an insult to the Canadian people, and it is an insult to the hundreds of thousands of unemployed men and women walking the streets of Canada today looking for work.
This budget does nothing to help the low and middle income Canadian taxpayers. On the contrary, through the maintenance of the surtax when it was supposed to be eliminated, when we were all assured that was to be the case and when everybody was counting on it, the budget hurts everybody. Our approach would have been one of selective tax reductions, once again with the aim of engendering confidence. But the government has refused to do so, and once again I say the government is wrong.
This is a sort of go-it-alone budget, one that assumes rather arrogantly that only the government can be trusted with anything, even if it is precious little, that only the government can be trusted to do anything about economic expansion. The budget ignores the contributions of Canadians, whether they be taxpayers or businessmen. The budget ignores the contributions that Canadians can make through their own efforts and through their own decisions.
This is a budget that does nothing to encourage confidence in the economy, the sort of confidence that can lead to expansion and to growth. True, the government speaks in optimistic words, but we have seen enough of this government's lack of foresight to realize that these are words and nothing more. The government can fool itself, but it is not going to fool anybody else. What was needed was not words but action to demonstrate the government's confidence in the economy. There was not any. That was the true eloquence of that speech, a very unfortunate sort of eloquence, if I may say so.
This is a budget that clearly falls between two stools. In terms of the serious and immediate situation this winter, including the prospect of the worst unemployment situation in a decade, this budget is virtually useless, and in terms of long term economic planning it is virtually meaningless. It gives no hint of what, if any, long term plans the government has. This budget is totally devoid of meaning. Perhaps we will have another budget in January, I do not know. The budget is a mish-mash of unrelated, mostly insignificant measures that neither give any hope for the solution of immediate problems nor provide any guidelines for the future of our economy.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and other opposition speakers so far have called for a number of measures which I wholeheartedly endorse. These include the abolition of the surtax, the immediate relief for low income wage earners-which the government itself has claimed to favour-a reduction in the federal sales tax on building materials, and an emergency amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to temporarily increase the period of benefits and reduce the qualifications during the coming winter.

Sir, these are practical proposals. They are the sort of proposals that we were expecting the government to bring forward when it announced it was going to bring down a budget, because when it made that announcement we assumed the government had something useful to contribute. Instead, we have a document that, I am sorry to say, is quite worthless in terms of facing up to the very grave problems we are facing today.
The Financial Times summed up the situation, I think, very nicely in an editorial this week, and I quote:
Mr. Benson's budget last Thursday may not have disappointed everybody in Canada. No expectations were high and some pessimists expected less than others. But Mr. Benson must have administered the greatest possible disappointment to the largest number of people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sir, this is a disappointing document. This is an arrogant, complacent document. But it is one that once again shows the Canadian people the true face of the government. I am only sorry that the Canadian people have to pay so high a price to have a glimpse of the reality that is behind the fine words which we have been served so long.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the budget that was not going to be brought down, in order to deal with the unemployment situation which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) says does not exist, and to improve the economy that the government says is progressing satisfactorily. Certainly, that is the conclusion anyone would come to who reads the speech of the Minister of Finance when presenting this budget last Thursday. That speech, Mr. Speaker,
would lead one to believe that the Minister of Finance is living in a world of make believe. As reported at page 1738 of Hansard he says:
-unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis appears to be falling.
Surely, the minister has to be kidding. It is true he can hang that statement on a technicality because the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate from September to October dropped from 6.9 per cent to 6.6 per cent. However, he fails to point out that at the end of October there were 419,000 unemployed, that this figure is 21,000 higher than the previous month, and 105,000 higher than the same month of the previous year.
On the same page the minister is reported as saying:
The national accounts for the third quarter also reveal that real output in the economy is rising.
Later, on the same page, he is reported as saying:
-this latest information confirms that the economy is now advancing again-
But in the same speech, Mr. Speaker, the minister admits that budgetary revenues are expected to decline by $100 million below what had been forecast, which is surely an unfailing sign of a slackening in the economy. The fact is that the national economy is stagnant. There has been hardly any real growth since last spring. After allowing for taxes and rising prices, the average real personal income of Canadians actually dropped in the first half of this year.
It should be pointed out that the minister's optimism is in glaring contrast to statements made by Mr. Arthur Smith, Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, in a speech which he made in Montreal on December 2. On that occasion the Chairman of the Economic Council said: Thus a significant portion of our national production resources are now running to waste-in total, perhaps at an annual rate of about $4 billion. In other words, on the average, in each week in the latter part of 1970, perhaps about $75 million to $80 million of output is not being produced that could potentially be produced, and an equivalent amount of total income that could potentially be earned is not being generated.
In the same speech, the Chairman of the Economic Council went on to point out that it would require an increase in real output of about 10 per cent to take the economy back to about 4 per cent unemployment by early 1972. To achieve our potential output by 1973 would require a 7.5 per cent growth rate in each of the next two years. I point out that this is a totally different prognosis of our economy from that which has been given to the House by the Minister of Finance. We have already had a bill to gag the Auditor General. Perhaps we shall now be confronted with legislation to silence the Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, whose economic forecasts have been conspicuously accurate and whose warnings the government has consistently ignored. In his speech the minister said, and I quote:
We are in fact having a considerable boom in housing in Canada-
This is mainly due to massive pump priming by the government. But the 270,000 housing starts to which the

December 8, 1970

minister referred should be set in their proper perspective. At the beginning of the year the government set as an objective the construction of 200,000 houses. This was later revised downward to 180,000 houses. The last reports indicate that this goal will not be reached, and that the figure is more likely to be in the neighbourhood of 165,000 homes completed in 1970.
The minister contends that rising prices have been curbed, but this has been largely due to the drop in food prices with disastrous results for the farming population. The slowdown in price increases has been bought at the price of an economic slowdown and an unemployment rate that is the highest in the western world. The truth is that the Prices and Incomes Commission has abandoned its guidelines as a colossal failure because the government lacked the courage to impose selective mandatory controls in the sensitive areas of the economy. The government has consistently followed what I would call a stop-go policy. Instead of pursuing a policy that has clear cut goals and objectives which the Canadian people could understand and foster, the government's economic policy has been one of fits and starts.
In 1967 a former minister of finance, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), said the economy was like a car that had been going too fast, and that we must now take our foot off the gas and put it on the brake. Six months later he took his foot off the brake and put it back on the gas, and a few months later he had it back on the brake again. In 1968 the government decided to put its foot on the brake with a vengeance and introduced monetary and fiscal restraints. It was warned by the Economic Council of Canada, by some of the best economists in the country, by newspaper editors and by members of the opposition, that these restraints would inevitably lead to an economic recession. As late as a few weeks ago when the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Donald MacDonald, warned that unemployment could reach 9 per cent this winter, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not only questioned the accuracy of these figures but questioned Mr. MacDonald's veracity. For the past year danger signals have been flashing, but the government has consistently refused to see them. Rumour has it that the Prime Minister is annoyed with some of the economists in the Department of Finance for not warning the government of the impending unemployment crisis. Yet the government has no one to blame but itself. It has consistently refused to listen. Consequently, this country faces a very grim winter indeed.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The government was asked questions in the House as to whether any new measures would be introduced to deal with the unemployment situation. The answer was no. They were asked whether unemployment insurance benefits would be increased. The answer was no. They were asked if the government would implement a winter works program. Again, the answer was no. Having said no to all these proposals, the Minister of Finance is belatedly trying to put them into effect by bringing down this budget.
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas
However, the budget, I submit, is too little and too late. Because of the time lag, through which it takes between four and six months for policies to become effective in providing jobs, the action taken by the government now will do little to provide employment this winter. It is to be hoped that it will provide some benefit in 1971.
This stop-go policy has caused irreparable damage to our economy. We have lost production in the last two years that can never be recovered. The government have been jumping from the brake to the accelerator, going when they should be stopping and stopping when they should be going.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And going into reverse.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now
they have put their feet on the brake and the accelerator at one and the same time, with the result that the car has stalled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It stalled because they went into reverse.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The
Minister of Finance will be known as the "great miscal-culator". He has been wrong in almost every prediction that he has made.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take away his driver's licence.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He has
landed this country in an economic mess. If he had lived a few hundred years ago under an absolute monarchy-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps he did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-he
would have been demoted from keeper of the King's purse to keeper of the royal chamber pot.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everything in this country has gone to pot.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This budget should have been aimed at getting the country going again. In order to do this, the government would need two basic approaches: first, an expansionist program to put the unemployed to work; second, a redistribution of purchasing power to stimulate the economy by creating effective demand. It is for this reason that the members of the New Democratic Party have been advocating repeatedly that the government should use large expenditures for the purpose of stimulating housing, the construction of schools and hospitals and other items of high social priority. We have urged that financial help be granted to the unemployed, to the old age pensioners, to

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas those on veterans pensions and to the recipients of war veterans' allowances. We have pressed for a reduction of tax payments for the low and middle income groups. This would have had the effect of redistributing income.
What have been the government's solutions with respect to these proposals? First, let us see what they have done about expanding the economy to put the unemployed to work. Belatedly, now, they are going to spend some money on public works. Twenty million dollars has been allocated for roads to the international airport at Montreal, and $23 million for the rest of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Big deal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, big deal. This is a pathetic gesture, like throwing a sardine to a hungry whale. They are proposing to spend $40 million for housing. This will help, but it falls far short of what is required. No action is being taken to reduce the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials at a time when the lumber industry, which depends for 80 per cent of its business on the export trade, in facing a 6 per cent increase in costs as the result of the rise of the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar.
The government has proposed setting up a $150 million capital loan fund, from which the provincial governments can draw for public works. Mr. Speaker, the premier of Quebec first made these proposals last June in Winnipeg, at the federal-provincial conference. He called for a fund to be utilized for both grants and loans. The grants were to increase for the provinces with the highest unemployment and the loans would be a smaller part of the contribution which they would receive. What the provinces are to receive are not grants at all, but loans entirely, loans to be lent at very high rates of interest. No wonder Premier Bourassa is reported in the press as having said that, "The budget is insufficient to deal with Quebec's problems."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us
see what this fund is to do in putting the unemployed to work. It is to be spread over 16 months. Quebec is to get $68 million, and $28 million of that amount this winter. British Columbia will get $35 million, and of that amount $13 million this winter. Ontario will get $17 million, and $6 million this winter. Manitoba will get $8 million and $3 million this winter. Saskatchewan and Newfoundland will each get $5 million, and of that they will get $2 million this winter. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are to get $4 million, and of that $1.5 million this winter. Prince Edward Island will get $1 million. Mr. Speaker, does anyone really think that these amounts of money will enable provinces to cope adequately with the problem of unemployment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance seems to think so.
[Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By
refusing to give this money in the form of grants as opposed to loans, the federal government has merely passed the buck to the provinces, which must now increase their debts and debt charges in order to receive amounts of money that will do little to help them solve the problems of the unemployed.
Let us see what the government is doing about the matter of redistributing purchasing power. We all expected, of course, that the 3 per cent surcharge on personal income and corporate tax would be dropped, because it was due to expire at the end of this month. The government has announced that the tax is to be retained. Mr. Speaker, this budget was not necessary. The public works items in it could have been included in the supplementary estimates, and members of the government could have made statements on motions. Why was this budget brought down? This budget is a farcical charade designed to conceal the reimposition of the 3 per cent surcharge which the minister said only six weeks ago would not be reimposed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This whole structure has been built up as a budget to conceal the fact that the government was going to continue taking from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada $245 million a year. That money ought to have been allowed to remain in their pockets so that they could buy goods to stimulate the economy and create effective demand in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A nice Christmas present the taxpayers have been given.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By
creating effective demand, the government could stimulate the economy more effectively than by making available some of the write-offs and capital cost allowances which it proposes to hand out. These, the minister tells us, are going to cost the taxpayers of this country some $250 million. There has been no reduction of taxes in the lower and middle income groups. The least that could have been done was to have exempted from taxation single persons earning $2,000 a year or less and married couples earning $4,000 a year or less. The government has not done that. This is why we have moved an amendment criticizing the government for failing to do this. Even those in receipt of the guaranteed supplement will have to pay income tax on a pension which leaves them far below the poverty line.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Instead of raising pensions for those in receipt of the basic old age pension, as of January 1 their pensions will be reduced by $1.17 a month. Under the present legislation those receiving the basic pension would be entitled to a cost of living bonus which would have increased their pension to $81.17 a month. The government is
December 8, 1970

to freeze their pension at $80. What does this mean? Assuming that the cost of living increases by at least 2 per cent, and it will probably increase more than that, at the end of five years they will be receiving $9 a month less in actual purchasing power than they would have received if the legislation now on the statute books had been left alone.
It seems unbelievable that the government would freeze the basic old age pension and refuse to grant a cost of living bonus to these people. No other group coming under federal jurisdiction is denied a cost of living bonus. Retired civil servants, military personnel, Members of Parliament, Senators and those receiving the Canada Pension Plan all have a built-in cost of living bonus in their retirement plan. Only the old people are discriminated against.
What is the government saving? It is saving $15 million a year. Contrast this with capital cost allowances to industry which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) estimates will cost the treasury $250 million. The government cannot find $15 million a year to give a cost of living bonus to the old people, but it can find $250 million to hand out to industry through write-offs. This is in keeping with the Liberal philosophy, "take care of the corporate structure and the corporate structure will take care of you."
Increased pensions for veterans and recipients of the guaranteed supplement will not come into effect until April 1, 1971. This will do nothing to help these people eke out an existence during the coming winter months. It will do nothing to help stimulate the economy at a time when it is in the doldrums. One cannot escape the conclusion that the government is callously unconcerned about what happens to the old people, the veterans and the unemployed during this winter. Their plans are aimed at an economic upswing during the latter part of 1971 in the fond hope that the economy will be rolling again by 1972. Such cynicism is unhumane and inexcusable. I am convinced that the Canadian people are not likely to forget this attitude.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the supplementary budget tabled last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brings nothing new but that it indicates the government has abandoned its policy of balancing the budget.
Over the last few years, both the government and the Minister of Finance have spoken very highly of the benefits to be derived from a balanced budget.
With a strong government, they said, there will be no more adverse budgets. The government was to take every step to insure maximum administrative efficiency.
All the afore-mentioned, Mr. Speaker, was to bring us a just society and a balanced budget. Those promises were made throughout the country and widely publicized, and Canada was to enjoy after that all the pleasures of the Garden of Eden.
The Budget-Mr. Rodrigue
That period was short, barely long enough to launch the publicity and inform the population. We just got to see the outside of that famous paradise, that is to say the fence in front of which some flowers had been planted for show.
Yet the Minister of Finance was so optimistic in his budget speeches of the last two years. Nevertheless last Thursday, as he announced a deficit, the Minister of Finance kept his smile and his confidence. Confidence in what? I wonder.
The minister talked of strategy, of economic objectives, of improving the income of Canadians, of guiding the economy toward high and sustained expansion, of eliminating regional economic disparities, of a more equitable distribution of goods and services and of several other matters. How conceited! There is no doubt that those objectives offer interesting features and are sought by all Canadians.
[DOT] (4.30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I am positive that all members, whatever their political affiliations, are wishing for the same thing as the hon. minister and that they approve of the objectives. We hope these expectations will materialize and progress beyond the stage of wishful speeches. Otherwise, we will be bound to believe that the minister has joined the ranks of meteorologists who are always so sure of their long-term forecasts which in any case prove to be partly right in the long run.
So, this is a return to the adverse budget policy. When the budget was introduced last March, a surplus was forecast but now it so happens that the Minister of Finance is speaking of a $570 million deficit for the current year. Even if the minister while forecasting a deficit has no new taxes to announce except for the extension of the 3 per cent surtax, or social development tax, until December 31, 1971, an adverse budget points to new taxes later on. This is not for the coming months, of course, but new taxes will have to be levied some day, because deficits cannot be covered by borrowing only. So, there will be an increase of the national tax and of course, interest also will have to be paid on these borrowings, because as far as I know, the minister has yet to make the decision of asking the Bank of Canada to finance public projects on an administration cost basis.
For the time being, the government deals with liquidity problems, without caring too much for the future. A few weeks ago, it floated a $550 million bond issue, at rates of 5J, 6 and 7 per cent depending on the term of the loan. It was said on the prospectus of this issue that the capital from the bonds would be used for the redemption of $375 million worth of maturing on Canadian government bonds on December 15, 1970 and for general expenditure purposes of the Government of Canada, including advances to the Canadian National Railway for the reimbursement of $40 million in bonds maturing on January 16, 1971, at a rate of 25 per cent.
The amounts borrowed to redeem bonds at maturity are ever increasing, in fact, they are even greater than the amounts to be redeemed, as well as the rates of

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Rodrigue
interest. That is what budget deficits lead us to: ever increasing debts and rates of interest, to the extent where servicing the debt-14.1 per cent of the budget-ranks third immediately following health, which represents 23.7 per cent, and regional economic expansion, 13.7 per cent. It will not be long before servicing the debt ranks second among budget expenditures.
The 10 per cent increase in unemployment insurance announced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), which is provided for in the budget, will certainly be welcomed by the recipients. That step will enable them to meet part of their needs. By taking that step, the government recognizes the seriousness of the situation. They also recognize the fact that the programs announced in the budget will have no beneficial effect on the economy before several months.
Let us not delude ourselves about the results of the programs that have been announced: several months will go by before all the preliminary steps have been taken, so that the amounts given for this year will in effect be carried over to 1971.
While admitting that higher unemployment insurance benefits will put additional purchasing power into the hands of jobless consumers, we should not forget those people who are not entitled to these benefits, those who are no longer eligible or will soon cease and those who have never been eligible for one reason or another. Those people will not benefit from the 10 per cent increase and we know that there are many of them.
The Minister of Labour stated in his press release of December 3, and I quote:
The 10 per cent increase in benefit rates will put a total amount of $54 million into the hands of the unemployed. This increase in their purchasing power will help stimulate the economy.
We agree with this statement. For years we have been repeatedly asking that the consumer's purchasing power be increased so that no action from the government will be necessary as regards production or investment.
It is astonishing that before suggesting a 10 per cent increase in the unemployment insurance benefits, the minister did not ask himself certain questions. In fact he did not say: Those benefits cannot be increased because they will create inflation. He did not hesitate. He did not say I am sorry, we cannot do it, there are not enough products, dairy products are scarce, grain is scarce, Canada is short of clothing. I am sure he did not even think of that. Indeed, he was quite pleased to make this announcement because he knew that it would be well received.
When the Minister of Finance said, in beginning his speech, that employment in Canada is rising, I think he was contradicting himself. If employment is rising, why has it been decided to raise unemployment insurance benefits and to announce the introduction of new programs? It is high time the real problem should be recognized.
More precisely, the Minister of Finance declared, some time ago in Alberta, that unemployment has become the
government's No. 1 enemy. In saying so, the minister confessed to his own failure.
During the year 1970, large corporations have laid off at least 10,000 workers in the province of Quebec only. In my view, these figures are conservative since lay-offs in large corporations outside Quebec have not been taken into account. Among the larger corporations, Can-adair has laid off nearly 3,150 workers during the year 1970 and has announced another 350 lay-offs before the end of the year.
Canadian Marconi has laid off 800 workers since the beginning of the year.
In the Quebec City area, Industries Valcartier, a general Investment Corporation subsidiary, will lay off 500 persons before the end of the year.
On the other hand, the United Aircraft Corporation has reduced its staff from 5,400 employees to 4,850 since the beginning of the year.
In the last six months, some six companies in Drum-mondville have closed their doors or have laid off nearly 800 workers.
Recently, the Wabasso Corporation has been laying off employees in Grand'Mere and Trois-Rivieres.
This is the situation in the field of employment. All the investment programs which have been announced will be beneficial in the long term. But this does not solve our present short-term problems.
Before investing or capitalizing in excess, we must also think of consuming.
Adoption of the sub-amendment now being considered which aims at raising personal tax exemptions to $2,000 for single persons and $4,000 for married persons would be a positive action allowing people with insufficient income to increase their purchasing power, consume more and leave in the economy an important sum of money. I will therefore support this sub-amendment without qualification.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to say a few words on the extension of the General Adjustment Assistance Program to the footwear industry. That program will not solve all our problems. I agree with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who believes that certain industries must modernize and recycle their production. That is true, but the great problem now is not so much that of modernization, because I know certain industries which have spent considerable sums of money in recent years to modernize their plants and which are in a position to produce a very large quantity of shoes everyday. Yet, despite all that modernization, those industries are facing problems because for a few years now we have been importing very large quantities of shoes from countries where salaries are low and where they still use manufacturing processes given up here many years ago. I have even learned that in some countries, certain phases of the manufacturing of shoes were given to women who did part of their work at home during their spare time.

December 8, 1970

Thus by proceeding in that manner, it is obvious that goods can be marketed at a lower price and I do not believe that, even if the government is ready to pursue notable endeavours in the way of modernization, it will be in a position to definitely solve the problem confronting the shoe industry, especially if it merely grants subsidies to the manufacturers or guarantees their borrowings. In fact, from 1956 to 1969, footwear imports increased by 568 per cent, reaching in 1968 the record volume of 46 million pairs of shoes.
Now, I believe that the problem is acute, especially considering that skilled shoe industries are located in areas where unemployment is quite high and where wages fall below the Canadian average. Therefore, measures other than the assistance made available for modernizing machinery should be introduced because the existing uneasiness in the footwear industry has significantly contributed to boost unemployment in several areas this year. I consider that it is high time to act before it is too late.
There are many other points that I should like to touch upon and that I feel very important, including construction. As many others, I had hoped that the Minister of Finance would announce at least some reduction in the sales tax on building materials. This would have been a tremendous encouragement to construction in some areas of the province of Quebec as well as in the whole country.
The government did promise to provide an additional $40 million in the field of construction. This amount will be used to build some 4,000 housing units. Frankly, considering the housing needs in Canada, it can be seen that those $40 million cannot solve the problem.
Once more I express the wish that the Minister of Finance seriously consider the possibility of abolishing the sales tax on building materials. I hope he will bring forward in a few months, before the next budget, bills to assist those who need a home. Reducing or abolishing that tax would be a great step toward the solution of Canada's housing problem.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
