subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand my Parliamentary Secretary did a good job, but perhaps the hon. gentleman will do better next time. I would rather talk about unemployment insurance and the contributions that will flow from the increased benefits that come into effect on January 1, namely the 10 per cent increase in benefits for people on unemployment insurance.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was kind enough yesterday to ask some basic questions about why the Minister of Labour had recommended that the government follow the procedure of increasing the size of the benefits rather than extending the period of benefits for the winter months. I must admit that the alternative suggested in the question of the hon. gentleman had been thoroughly discussed within the department but rejected in favour of increasing benefits, and for fairly logical reasons that I should like to explain.
One of the reasons is this. If not for logical reasons certainly for historical reasons, and because of climatic conditions, we have paid in the winter months what is known as seasonal benefits. Seasonal benefits, as most members of the House already know, provide a method for extending unemployment insurance benefits to those unemployed who, under normal circumstances, would not be eligible for benefits for a variety of reasons-for example, perhaps not enough stamps in their book, indicating insufficient attachment to the work force before becoming unemployed.
Because we already have in the existing plan this feature that permits the Unemployment Insurance Commission the maximum degree of latitude with regard to extending existing benefits to those people who normally would not be drawing any benefits, it was felt that it might be in the best interests of the economy, and of the people drawing unemployment insurance in particular, that these benefits be increased by 10 per cent.

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
I think it is significant, too, that the $54 million will not be taken out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund but will be taken from general revenue. This simplifies the introduction of this change and prevents the necessity for legislation. In addition, it removes the temptation on anyone's part to suggest that the 10 per cent increase, or the $54 million, should at the same time be accompanied by an increase in contributions.
I think this particular feature of the budget that was announced by the minister the other eveming should meet with general approval from the House. Let me make it quite clear that it helps only certain of the unemployed, those who are temporarily without earnings, rather than the chronic unemployed, the underemployed, or people who unfortunately have to live off assistance and welfare. Nevertheless this immediate injection into the economy of $54 million should in some way help to provide some of the spending power that I think we need if we are going to stimulate the economy in the immediate future to any great degree.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I think the Minister of Finance has already pointed out in greater detail than I could, and I do not intend to repeat, the other features that were announced during the week prior to the budget. I have in mind the increase in war veterans' allowance pensions, and in basic pensions, GIS, etc, all plans which eventually will put into the hands of people many at the bottom level of the income scale in Canada the type of income they need and deserve.
I might sound rather like a heretic if I were to suggest that a country as rich as Canada should never again be faced with this degree of unemployment. People today are interested in the quality of life rather than quantity of life. A better educated work force and, paradoxically, a better educated non-working force will no longer tolerate the booms and busts of our economy. They have been synonymous with most of the economies of what is loosely known as the western world. The targets of this and all future governments should at all times be full employment. I think I am really echoing the sentiments of the cabinet in general, and certainly those of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in saying that, everything being equal, this government is dedicated to the concept of full employment.
Full employment is a matter of definition, of course. The Economic Council defines it as 3 per cent unemployment. Others define it as 3.5 per cent, and the actual records I have from 1962 probably indicate that the rate of unemployment in the last decade has been between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. I might indicate as well, in case the opposition feels a little smug or complacent about their own record, that between the years 1958 and 1962 the rate of unemployment in this country surpassed 7 per cent. I am not trying to be partisan by this remark but there is a parallel between the problems which confronted Canada between 1958 and 1962 and the problems that face the country at the present moment.
Behind unemployment, or contributing to it, has been the repetition or recurrence of inflation. Among our economists, at least those of whom favour, Galbraith, Friedman, Keynes, there is a difference of opinion as to how to control inflation. Traditionally, the manner in which it has been controlled in most countries associated with the International Monetary Fund and similar organizations has been by fiscal and monetary policies.
The Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson warned a year or so ago that fiscal and monetary policy control inevitably and unfortunately led to unemployment. It seems to me, as a person who does not claim to be an economist, that the time has come when economists both in the government and outside find a better way of controlling inflation and replace measures that unintentionally put Canadians out of work. I think speakers on both sides of the House have indicated the terrible toll this takes and the lack of productivity it generates. There is a greater need at this time for a better way when the work force of this country, both employed and unemployed, is demanding a better quality of life. People today no longer will tolerate slums or accept unemployment. They will not tolerate pollution and exploitation.
Perhaps one of the phenomena of the present decade, and certainly of the future, is that the people have the media to communicate their discontent. Perhaps what has been overlooked by the House is that as far back as the month of March the Minister of Finance predicted the problems with which we are now faced. In the month of March the government released considerable sums of money into the economy. The chartered banks of the country today have more than ample money available for lending, and interest rates have decreased substantially. This was not the result of action taken last week but the result of action taken last March. This indicates that the Minister of Finance was doing the proper things as far back as March to stimulate the economy, to control unemployment and to reduce the always terrible spectre of inflation which, in the final analysis, is as equally demoralizing as a high rate of unemployment.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the leader of the NDP as well, as other hon. members in the opposition, are and will logically be talking about the problem of unemployment. They talk about people on fixed incomes and our senior citizens. I am as aware of these people as they are. I am not unaware of what inflation does to these people on fixed incomes. All of us realize there is a limit to what a country of this size with 20 million people can do in the form of desirable social measures. This is a country of many regions with many regional disparities. It does not have the productive capacity of the United States. Certainly, anything is economically possible in a time of full employment. I think the message we should be getting is that we cannot expect both a high rate of unemployment and the high measure of social assistance this country desires and expects. Certainly, none of us appreciates or feels comfortable with certain fiscal and monetary policies that control inflation but result in higher unemployment.
Mr. Mackasey.]
December 8, 1970

There is no point in any member of the opposition or anyone else presuming that inflation was not one of the great problems this country has been faced with in the last year or so. It is all too easy to forget that it still lurks around the comer. Learned economists still point out that unless we are very careful, the reinjection of money to prime the pump, as somebody has said, such as money needed to increase housing starts for instance, is a factor that contributes to inflation. I might also mention the $54 million which will be put into the economy this winter and the $150 million the provinces will be using for winter works, as well as the reduction in interest rates designed to stimulate operations and expand the economy, all are potential factors in recreating inflation.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
One thing intrigued me more than anything else in these contributions to which I have listened today. I refer to the contribution of the leader of the New Democratic Party who on many occasions has emphasized the need for selective controls in the future. This could be the answer. I have heard him use this expression on half a dozen occasions in this House. To this extent, we know that he is sincere in speaking of selective controls. I have heard him on radio and television speak of the use of selective controls. I have never heard him tell us precisely in what areas he would use his selective controls. I do not know whether he would advocate controls in respect of abnormally high wages in the construction area. I do not know whether this is one area he would consider. In all probability, he would place selective controls on the chartered banks of the country. In line with the philosophy or what used to be the philosophy of that party-I am not sure what it is these days but presumably it is the philosophy before the waffle group takes over-I presume the selective controls in this country would be in general against big business just as if big business has no place in the economy.
Big business does generate jobs and the opposition must realize that if we are to have the social policies this country needs, and if we are to create the jobs we need for perhaps the fastest growing force in the world, we will have to encourage Canadian investors, multinational and international corporations to invest in this country, preferably along guidelines that will protect the Canadian economy and prevent further erosion of Canadianism. Nevertheless, I think the suggestion of the hon. gentleman who leads the New Democratic Party that we should be prepared to introduce selective controls might very well be the answer to the next round of inflation. The point I am getting at is that this country can no longer afford the type of unemployment that faces us this winter.
If an unemployment figure of 3 per cent historically has been equated with full employment or what is commonly called the trade-off point or the emergence of inflation, then from that point on, if we are to have full employment, it is obvious that we will have to find something other than simply fiscal and monetary policies with which to conquer inflation. It may be that selective controls would be a solution. Certainly, this would be
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
preferable to massive unemployment. We may have to introduce controls. They may be selective controls, as Galbraith suggests, over key industries and over key trade unions or over the unions which operate in the key industries such as the steel industry, the automotive industry, the chemical industry and others. He suggests these unions should be controlled because their agreements affect the service industries and the effect on these industries breeds dissension among the low-income workers, so the spiral starts all over again. I do not know whether these are the selective controls to which the hon. member alluded, but they are the controls referred to by Galbraith.
The other method by which to control inflation is voluntary restraint. I think we have gone through a period which indicates that this approach leaves a lot to be desired because there were not too many volunteers. There were very few volunteers in the professional ranks. There were not too many landlords who were prepared to roll back rents. There were not many professional associations, such as architects and engineers, that were willing to roll back their fees. There were not too many people in the medical profession who thought they should reduce their fees. So obviously the villain of the piece was identified as organized labour. The method of voluntary restraint leaves much to be desired because it requires not only the full co-operation of some of the groups I have mentioned, but also requires the full and absolute co-operation of the provinces since we live in a federal state. It is unfair to select labour as the villain of the piece in respect of the workability of voluntary restraint. It is also unfair to presume that the Prices and Incomes Commission did not have any effect on prices.
If the Prices and Incomes Commission had no effect on prices, then big businesses would be tripping over themselves to re-endorse the concept because so long as they endorsed the concept and labour did not it was very easy for them to pinpoint labour in respect of its inability or unwillingness to co-operate. The fact that big business has not re-endorsed the Prices and Incomes Commission is an indication that this commission did have an effect, if only a psychological effect, on prices. With the new policy it will be interesting to see whether or not prices will remain within bounds over the next year or year and a half.
I believe the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will come into effect in July represent legislation which is long overdue. I believe this is the feeling of the committee which is composed of members of all parties in the House. Certainly the co-operation has been extraordinary. The points of difference have been very few. I believe this is a realistic approach to unemployment, or to the problems in respect of a particular group of unemployed, those who are temporarily unemployed or temporarily without earnings.
This legislation is not intended to be, nor will it ever need to be, a substitute for a guaranteed annual income. Nor, indeed, will it be the instrument by which to look at the problems with regard to the permanently disabled, the permanently unemployed or people without work for

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
long periods of time. But at least the benefits under this new plan which will be related to income will permit the person temporarily out of work to seek work without the problems which plague people who draw the rather low benefits which the unemployment insurance plan now provides. At the present time there are too many Canadians who happen to live off two cheques, one from the Unemployment Insurance office and another from the Canada Assistance Plan or local welfare. The new plan, if adopted and if the standing committee report does not basically change it, will do a good deal to remedy this. There is one feature in it which ought to appeal to members of the House. This is the fact that the government will absorb the cost of the plan once it reaches 4 per cent seasonally adjusted.
I do not believe members quite appreciate precisely what this means. When, for reasons best known to the economists or to the government, the unemployment figure may hit anywhere up to 7 per cent, the cost to the government would be $433 million. Certainly, this is a sum which may make people wish to review a little more closely what we call the trade-off factor. I think this regulatory feature is one of the better features of the new plan.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In conclusion let me say that I think the time is approaching when the problem of inflation should be tackled on a tripartite basis. I think that some medium of communication between labour, management and government is imperative in the future. There have been such talks of course at private levels. I have participated in some of it, and some of the viewpoints that have been advanced by economists attached to the labour movement have been very enlightening, very fruitful and very progressive. But I do not think that organized labour can stand back and divorce themselves from the problems of this country any more than big business can expect to operate in isolation without any humanitarian approach to the problems. I am not particularly pleased when multinational corporations close up plants in Cornwall or London, Ontario, with a minimum of advance notice and with little or no concern for the plight of the people whom they put out of work.
These are the type of responsibilities that private enterprise must assume in the future because there is more on trial than just the government or the opposition. In effect, the whole system is on trial, and people want more out of the private enterprise system than just a job and 4 per cent or 5 per cent rate of unemployment. They want full employment; they want social measures; they want an end to slums and pollution and all the other social evils. The message that all of us should get is that unless we are capable of taking up this kind of challenge we are going to be hardpressed to maintain this kind of private enterprise system which I happen to think is the best for our economy, despite what the socialists may think. We need and will see more and more government intervention and government participation in the decisions over the next decade. We can no longer afford inflation nor can we any longer afford abnormally high rates of unempoyment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I really had not expected to be called upon to speak in the House so soon, but it appears my colleagues in the official opposition have decided that, since I am here, they might as well put me to work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good idea.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would be an understatement to say that I am happy to be sitting in the House of Commons. What would perhaps be closer to the truth would be to say that I am overwhelmed. It is surely one of the greatest honours that can be accorded to any Canadian to be selected to representent a riding in this great country. Having said that, I hope hon. members will indulge me when I say that it is a particular honour to be chosen to represent the Lisgar riding in the province of Manitoba.
Hon. members will know that I came to the House of Commons as a result of a by-election following the untimely death of the previous member for Lisgar, George Muir. In his years in the House, George Muir earned the respect and regard of the people in his riding as well as of those who knew him in his capacity as a sitting member. I hope and trust that, as I mature in this job, those who selected me as his replacement will feel that they have made the right choice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This might be a good time to enlighten my colleagues as to the advantages of living in the Lisgar riding, and to invite them to take the first possible opportunity to avail themselves of our hospitality. Easterners are inclined to think of Vancouver, Edmonton or Calgary when mention is made of the west, but the fact is that the great Canadian west begins in Lisgar.
Lisgar riding stretches for about 130 miles from east to west, bounded on the south by the United States border and ending in the picturesque farmlands of a town called Killarney. Its eastern boundary follows the twists and turns of the Red River as it flows north from the United States border, and part of the northern boundary is the historic Assiniboine River. The Pembina River winds through Lisgar from west to east and flows into the Red River.
A large proportion of Lisgar riding comprises fertile land, and this, coupled with the fact that there are no large cities in the riding and very little industry, has resulted in an agriculture based economy in the riding. This can be both good and bad. In good times, when crop and livestock prices are high and there are good markets, life in Lisgar can be filled with all of the good things for which men and women strive. Conversely, when the agricultural economy in the country is in decline, the people of Lisgar would feel the effect a bit more than areas which enjoy an input from industries or resources. It could be said that in Lisgar we live with one anxious finger on the pulse of the agricultural economy.

December 8, 1970

People are the most important element in any riding, and I would like to speak for a moment, with justifiable pride, about the people in Lisgar. We have a situation that is fairly representative of agricultural communities in the country in that about 30 per cent of our people are 45 years of age or older. This is largely because we cannot provide adequately for the young people, talented and eager young people who want more than is available to them in a situation where the family farm is on the decline and there is no industry to absorb them. This is understandable, but it saddens me none the less, to see young people leave the rural life, not because it does not appeal to them but because there is no alternative.
About 40 per cent of the people in my riding are of British origin. Among them are some of the first families to settle in the area. About 11 per cent are of French Canadian origin, and it is the nature of the French Canadian to preserve his language and his culture wherever he settles. This has greatly enriched the culture of Lisgar, and we can consider that we benefit from the fact that we have the best of the two founding cultures of this great nation. We are also extremely proud of the people of Dutch ancestry who make up about 23 per cent of our number, and the 11 per cent of our riding who are of German origin. There are others, such as Poles, Ukrainians and Italians, to mention a few of the ethnic groups that grace our riding. We are indeed fortunate, and perhaps a little proud.
It is to the credit of the farmers of Lisgar riding that they saw the wisdom of diversification in agriculture long before the advent of the Lift program. Our people are not easily discouraged, and when it became apparent that farmers would have to adapt to new conditions and appeal to new markets if they were to survive, they began to diversify. They diversified because they wanted to survive. The people of Lisgar, for the most part, enjoy their way of life. The farm and the rural community are what they know best and what they like best, and they have decided that they will not easily be discouraged from holding on to the way of life that appeals to them.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I should mention in connection with that, Mr. Speaker, that about 80 per cent of the farm families in Lisgar live on the farm the year round. It is not just a business with them; it is their way of life. Many of the people I am talking about weathered the great depression. They came out of it poorer, but proud and more determined. Such people scoff at suggestions that they leave the farms for the cities, and we can ill afford to displace them, whatever the reason.
Much as I believe that the farm and the rural community are worth saving, and much as I believe that the headlong rush to the cities should be decelerated, I am not suggesting that we attempt to stop the clock. Progress is just as inevitable as death and taxes, and we in Lisgar want as much as anyone else to be a part of the great era of science and technology that lies before us. And we in Lisgar realize full well that we can do much to preserve our present environment by diversifying still further, and
The Budget-Mr. Murta
setting out to attract industry to bolster our local economy. At the same time that we are ensuring the continuance of those things that we want to keep, we might also encourage our young people to stay in our riding. The time has come when we need them. However, we must ensure that we not only keep them but that in future, when they look back, they will be glad they stayed.
To attract industry, a riding must have a labour force and an abundant supply of good water. We have the labour force and the water in Lisgar, but the water flows through our riding into the Red River and is lost. It is possible that at some future time my colleagues in this House will join with me in exploring ways that this water might be put to use in Lisgar. My predecessor was engaged in studies with regard to a series of dams on the Pembina River which would make supplies of water available to our agricultural region, and also provide the water reserves necessary to the development of industry. If a series of dams such as this could be built I have no doubt that industry and processing plants, as well as a new intense form of agriculture would emerge in Southern Manitoba.
Before I leave this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to dwell for just a moment on the aspect of agricultural people leaving the farm to find a new life in the city. By this I do not mean the young people who are just starting out in life. I am thinking about the people whose lives have been moulded, people who have spent a considerable part of their working lives in the agricultural economy, and who cannot easily adjust to an alien way of life. For the most part, these people would not have an opportunity to learn a new trade or profession, and would therefore be unable to compete in the job markets.
If it is necessary that these people should be relocated, and I concede that this will be necessary in many cases, then their prospects would be bleak indeed if we did not plan such moves very carefully in advance. I know many such people, and so I have a particular interest in what happens to them. They are for the most part proud individuals who have been used to working hard for what they receive. They would not take lightly to such remedies as welfare, and yet without training they would not have a chance in an alien environment. I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because this is an area in which I will take a special interest when I become fully involved in the affairs of the House. I do not suggest that I am in favour of accelerating the decline of the family farm as a part of the Canadian agricultural industry and as a way of life for those who prefer to live and work in the country. It just so happens that I think if our rural life is to continue it will be because of strong family farm units in rural areas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand fully that an uneconomic farm unit must be phased out of the economy, just the same as an uneconomic business or industry must fall by the way. I am hopeful that some means can be devised whereby as many as possible of our farm units can be preserved where people want to remain on the farm, and where

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Murta
such people can contribute to the success of their farm businesses with the application of sound management principles. Those who are forced to leave the farm should be trained for new jobs, and assisted until they are resettled.
While there are many advantages to living in Lisgar, Mr. Speaker, we are faced at the present time with the same problems that face the rest of the country. For that reason my people are understandably interested in what the federal government is doing and what it is proposing with respect to resolving farm problems. Now that I am in Ottawa, I expect that I will be getting letters and phone calls asking me what I am doing to help solve some of these problems.
Again, like the people in the rest of Canada, the farmers in my area are sorely beset by a shortage of cash to see them through the winter and to assist them in getting in the crops in the spring. Because of the nature of the farm industry in my riding, it appears that the corrective measures instituted thus far will have less effect than in some of the areas further west. However, I will be in a better position now to determine just what is being done and what is being planned.
Cash shortage in my riding is the result not only of slow movements of grain out of storage but is also the result of low market prices for hogs and other livestock. There is also a great deal of concern in my riding over the way the traditional markets for eggs and poultry have virtually dried up as a result of provincial restrictions imposed recently on the movement of eggs and poultry across provincial boundaries. I am hopeful that these problems will be resolved before permanent damage has been done to our traditionally stable markets.
Inasmuch as the entire economy of Lisgar is agriculture oriented, I hope sincerely that we will be able to devise some means of getting our farmers through the winter and spring. It is imperative that we do so if we are to head off economic disaster in rural ridings. I am not being an alarmist, Mr. Speaker; the situation is really that critical.
My colleagues will no doubt be happy to learn that I am about to conclude my remarks. I would guess that they are as happy as I am that I managed to get through my first speech without destroying the parliamentary system of government. I will try to correct that when I engage in serious debate in the future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying to my colleagues on both sides of the House that it has been most gratifying to have been received so warmly on my arrival here. I have been greatly encouraged by the kind of assistance that has been rendered me on every hand. Now that I am formally installed as a member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, I hope fervently that I will be here long enough and will conduct myself in such a manner that I will be able to feel
at some future time that my colleagues on both sides of the House are also my friends. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several things have already been said about the budget, but there is still a great deal to say. The main things have yet to be said. No mention at all has been made of logical solutions likely to settle our problems. The problems exist, but no solution is being proposed. Solutions are feared as if they were thunderbolts, but I shall take it upon myself to suggest some.
Every time the budget is brought down, reference is made to taxes and the taxpayers are even more burdened with taxes. Indeed, the administration takes in from 50 to 60 per cent of the income, so that the taxpayer is left with practically nothing.
In order to make money available to taxpayers, new loans must be raised and, consequently, more debts, that many more new burdens and difficulties which lead us to the worst failures on record. The more we move ahead, the more complicated the process becomes; as the rate of unemployment increases, so does dissatisfaction and also the trouble we have in solving our problems.
And all this is due to the fact that we ignore the true solutions to our problems. Once these problems are solved, it would be easier to provide for a sound administration.
Over the weekend, through the newspapers, I read some of the comments of various public and semi-public organizations on some aspects of the budget.
No general reduction in income taxes was announced, but a 10 per cent increase in unemployment insurance benefits was made official.
If we decide to increase unemployment insurance benefits, it is a sign that we are very far from the measures which should be passed to give the population what it is entitled to.
It was decided to continue for another year the surtax of 3 p. 100 on individual and corporate incomes. Well, Mr. Speaker, when one wants to relieve someone who has a very heavy load to carry, one makes his burden lighter rather than heavier. The situation is directly opposite in the present budget.
Nearly $150 million are granted to the provinces for job-creating projects, therefore laying at the door of the provinces the present difficulties because if they borrow $150 million they will have to pay an excessively high rate of interest.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had frozen the interest rate at 1 or 2 per cent, then it could have been said that he was truly willing to help the people instead of being partial to the financial sector. What he is doing now he is doing it for the latter at the people's expense as well as at the expense of the provinces already overtaxed and to whom further loans will only bring further difficulties.


December 8, 1970

Subsidies of $23 million are granted to the areas that have won the "unemployment Grey Cup" for the fight against unemployment and $20 million for building roads and facilities at the new airport. That makes sense because such things are necessary, but those are not the measures required to solve the problem of unemployment because machines are doing the work nowadays. In fact, only a few hundred workers will be hired for the construction of the international airport.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Chamber of Commerce of Canada, two of the most powerful organizations in the country, give the same interpretation to the budget statements of the Minister of Finance. Both say that the minister has chosen to give a little help instead of a moderate assistance to the economic development. Those are the words of Mr. J. C. Winthrop, vice-chairman of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
The newspaper La Presse of December 5 featured an article by Mr. M. K. Carthy, the Executive Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, who speaks along the same line. In both cases, they are experienced people whose opinion deserves respect.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of the few moments at my disposal to try and determine the constant cause of popular dissatisfaction over the budget that the minister has tabled.
Mr. Speaker, the estimates for our national production for the year 1970-71 are so favourable that they should allow all Canadians to enjoy a decent life. If we admit the importance of this production, on the other hand, we can state positively that it is not in keeping with the purchasing power of most Canadians.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
United Nations experts have many times called the Assembly's attention to the vicious circle in which the undernourished people find themselves.
According to them, malnutrition is one of the main causes of poor health in the Western world. And yet, we pay Western farmers to prevent them from growing grain, and that does not bother anybody, except those who are hungry. That makes them think.
The capacity to run into debt is greater than the ability to repay. Where are the reforms that the Minister of Finance or the government introduced to remedy the situation? Nobody notices anything and loses sleep over it. Discussions are held in order to go deeper into debt, while the old debts remain unpaid.
The government refuses to face facts. We are heading for complete failure because of our refusal to recognize that the problem is strictly economic, because we refuse to protect our economy by using our rights and prerogatives.
A time will come when new strategies will be planned because capitalism refuses to realize the meaning of the progressive discontent of frustrated populations. However, it is time to tell those who govern us to wake up, because they are dozing in the face of a dissatisfied society on the road to rebellion. The man who is natural-
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe
ly dedicated to justice revolts in the face of the present glaring injustice of our financial and fiscal systems. If we persist in ignoring the real objectives of community life, the real functions of the nations ministers and representatives, the fundamental structures of society will be undermined at the root and we shall witness the final collapse. The day this will happen may not be far away, and I am not hoping it will come. I am here today because I want reforms and because I see what is forthcoming. If others cannot see it, I do. Such are the conditions in which I speak before you now, in all awareness, anxious to assume my own responsibilities.
I regret that such a large number of Liberal and Conservative members have no solutions to offer to the government. It would still be possible to bring in the corrective measures needed within the framework of our conventional capitalism and stop communism from gaining ground.
We are fighting against poverty. Every attempt is made to balance our present economic system which generates poverty, but poverty persists. Departments and commissions are set up to determine whether poverty exists in Canada. This problem has been considered for many years.
When I was elected to the House in 1962, the Liberals were in the opposition. They were accusing the government of doing nothing to fight unemployment. They deplored the high unemployment rate, they denounced the misery of the people and they asked the government to take the necessary steps to put an end to it.
And the Conservative government passed all sorts of measures, including a winter works program, for instance, in the hope of protecting our citizens from unemployment and poverty. To this end, credit was loosened and the government had to run into deficit again and the Liberals inherited this situation when they took office. They said that the country was suffering from inflation and that it was absolutely necessary to take measures liable to cure it. But, in the guise of fighting inflation, they are pushing the Canadian people back into a state of dire need and they put our economy out of balance to an extent yet unknown in our country.
We are unable to avoid going from one economic recession to another. And even with stable governments, we have never succeeded in ensuring economic stability. Therefore, no stability, either with the Liberals or with the Progressive Conservatives. Indeed, we have known only unemployment, poverty and wars because we refuse to establish social justice as a means of distributing affluence instead of want.
The hon. Minister of Finance is now attempting to solve the present economic problem with his dropping-tube budget. Indeed, it takes more than a dropping-tube to eliminate the economic disorders we are now plagued with and that will plague us in the future if the government persists in generating want instead of distributing affluence.
We are not responsible enough to assume our responsibilities. Such an attitude is totally uncalled for.
The people are disatisfied with their traditional administrators, Liberals and Progressive-conservatives. The

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe
people are led up with old-line politics of backward and fossilized governments, unable to keep in tune with modern thought and science.
There is something wrong with the thinking of administrators, and any remedy is being cast aside. When one is well seated in an upholstered chair, when there is no problem at home, when a certain class of society is satisfied with the system, as are the big financial institutions
__because that system is a gold mine for them, even if
they operate at the expense of the little people-one can expect that the people will see to it one day. And that day, it will be a terrible disaster.
The dissent of students, and even the sensible recommendations of the new and less complacent political parties are as many symptoms of an uneasiness which will not disappear even through the most desperate efforts of an obsolete administration not attuned at all to our modem times.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Since the beginning of this century we have seen big industrial capital settling down in Canada and expanding so successfully for itself and for its millionaire and billionaire institutions; time has come to wonder whether all this show of power and production is actually meeting the rightful aspirations of our population.
Recent unusual events have forced this government to introduce unusual legislation.
Where are we heading to? The people are at a loss and are watching the government and the 264 ministers and Members of Parliament they have democratically elected to lead the country. This includes even the disserters and those who voted for the opposition members, including the impatients and the revolutionaries who are trying to get justice within a just society in Canada.
The unusual events that forced us to introduce an unusual legislation deserve at least being analyzed and studied with a view to finding their underlying reasons. And this is not being done. Let us think about it because when the bus is slowly skidding off the highway the driver should be wakened up and not the passengers. We are now trying to wake up the passengers because the driver is doing a bad job and refuses to take his own responsibilities to reach his goal.
This is a comparison. Normally when a passenger is travelling by bus no unusual events happen. Everybody reaches his destination and is quite satisfied with the trip made at an agreed price.
If the bus skids into the ditch, the passengers have reasons to be annoyed and dissatisfied, to seek out the people responsible for the unusual event and to ask at least to be led to their destination as established on departure.
If at the time of the last elections our citizens asked for a just society in a united Canada, they expect to live in such a society. They have reasons to be displeased if they see injustice everywhere, as well as a faulty distribution which makes the rich become richer and the poor poorer. They are also right when deploring unemployment and inflation, the exclusive privileges granted the large corporations, the hardship, want, insecurity and poverty prevailing among too large a sector of the population which, in its own way, contributes to the social, financial, economic and political life of the whole nation, according to its means and intellectual capacities.
The unwonted events which took place these last months should compel us to plead guilty and examine our conscience as to the way we guided the destiny of 22 million Canadians who paid to have a just society in a united Canada, as requested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who seems to be doing its utmost but who is always hindered in his action by traditions, red-tape and known or secret influences. It behooves us to support him in order to lead the state again towards justice, balance and harmony.
Mr. Speaker, when you administer a whole, you must take care of every part, because as everybody knows, the whole is made up of the parts. Canada is a whole which is made up of 21.5 million Canadians. These 21.5 million Canadians must be given a guaranteed income. Everywhere production is divided between consumption and capitalization. In all administration, revenue equals expenses plus profits. If we are to have a just administration, we must have revenue. In order to pay taxes and live decently, every citizen must have an income. And if the individual in society does not have sufficient income to cover his expenses, then there is unemployment and the undeserved poverty that we now have.
On behalf of all Canadians, I call upon hon. members to think deeply. In the name of justice, I call upon them to meet their responsibilities and to establish a fair system of justice based on economic reality. None of this was provided for in the budget, and few members strive towards social justice in Canada. I have come to the conclusion that they have no social conscience at all.
In 1970 production amounted to $84 billion. One should find in this amount expenses for $63 billion and benefits for $21 billion. That percentage of 75 and 25 should show up at the level of every single administration whether individual, domestic, social, municipal, provincial or federal. Everone should get his share of that production of $84 billion. Consumption should amount to $50 billion, and the capitalization surplus should amount to $34 billion. Capitalization is so considerable that citizens are denied a decent living standard. Part of it should be distributed within society. The Minister of Finance should have announced a reduction of the cost of living that is high at present because of ambitious people who capitalize too much.
The minister should have stepped in but unfortunately he still protects the big financiers. He is the enemy of the people because he does not assume his responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, before recess, I was saying that it would be easy to balance our economy if we would all co-operate.
The various white papers published up to now by the government, the Speech from the Throne in September 1970, the miniature budget brought in by the Minister of Finance on Thursday last, the investigation of the Senate committee on poverty as well as the eventual report that is not expected before next April, those are different indications that the economic system is sick and completely unbalanced on the whole as well as in its various forms of activity.
What should be the established order is organized disorder, planned economic unbalance. And all the efforts made to correct this situation do nothing but clog all the more the wheels of administration without in any noticeable way improving the results. Everyone does his best, under these circumstances, at each administrative level, but the main fault lies with those who lead, be they well known or unknown, elected by the people or by the shareholders of big financial, industrial or business corporations.
Mr. Speaker, I have drawn a table to shed a little light on ail the white papers proposed by various departments. This table is more eloquent than all the thick reports of the Royal Commissions on banks, unemployment, poverty, biculturalism and many other topics, which are so costly in time and money but very often do little more than increase the confusion in the minds of officials, ministers and departmental technocrats.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced his budget a few days ago we were encouraged by the many references he made to
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
regional development and particularly to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. We were encouraged because many of us in the House, indeed many throughout the country, have long held the view that in order for regional economic expansion programs to be effective in this country they must be co-ordinated with the government's monetary and fiscal policies.
We hope that the government is finally coming around to this viewpoint, because in order to have regional development policies that result in the creation of employment and the stabilization of the economy there must be this co-ordination with our monetary and fiscal policies. More particularly, if these regional development programs are to be truly effective in stabilizing the economy and creating employment, then they in turn must be truly regional in concept. We therefore welcome this change in government policy, noting at the same time that it is one we have advocated for some time.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
This concept is directed essentially toward the creation of employment opportunities in the regionally disadvantaged areas of the country. It is our belief that if you designate the whole country as a special area under a regional development incentives program, as my col-leage the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter) said you will end up, in fact, with no special areas and the program as a consequence defeats its very purpose. This is what we have been trying to tell the government since this program was first announced. As a result, we draw some encouragement from the fact that the minister announced in his budget speech that the government proposed to lift the ceiling on individual projects undertaken in the Atlantic provinces under the regional incentives program. Special incentives are essential if the area is to attract new industry or encourage plant expansion by existing industries.
We all know that industry has to take the initiative under this program, and we point this out as one of the major weaknesses in the program. If the initiative is left to industry, it will want to locate in areas close to major markets. This, we submit, is a major weakness in the program. The government, in announcing the special incentives for the Atlantic provinces-which we feel are essential if the area is to compete with other designated areas close to the major markets of the country-offset this advantage to the Atlantic region because in the same budget speech the government announced the designation of the city of Montreal and the southeastern area of Ontario as special areas. I submit it will take considerably more than the 10 per cent additional incentive for the Atlantic region, which the government has proposed, to offset this move.
I am not for a moment suggesting that unemployment is not seriously high in Montreal and the southeastern area of Ontario, because we all know it is. I am saying that the Atlantic provinces do not stand a chance under this program. There is no way they can compete with the advantaged areas of the country in terms of transportation and proximity to major markets. In this respect the Atlantic provinces are just not in the ball game. I am

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
very much afraid it will take a winter of hardship, as a consequence of probably the highest unemployment since the depression, to prove this point. This also applies to other areas of the country; I have in mind particularly northern Ontario and the Gaspe region of Quebec.
The proposed amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act will certainly improve the program; nobody would deny that. But it will not do so in so far as the regional disadvantaged areas of the country are concerned. I make special reference to my own province of Newfoundland. In this connection that province does not stand a chance. The only way industry will be induced to establish in the province of Newfoundland, with its transportation problems, is if the people of Newfoundland will assume all the risks involved in a new venture. We have evidence and many examples that this is a fact. The people must assume all the risks, thereby making it so attractive to promoters that they in fact have nothing to lose. The people of Newfoundland must assume all the risks which would normally be assumed by the entrepreneur. This added burden to the people of Newfoundland must automatically increase the already high burden of provincial debt. This is a debt which I submit is already critically high.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and the officials of his department seem to have been completely carried away. That is the only way one can explain the reason for this program which makes the whole of the country a designated area, to the economic disadvantage of regions which are now completely out of the economic picture, particularly areas such as the Atlantic provinces which had certain advantages prior to the coming into effect of this program. I refer to programs such as the Atlantic Development Board which gave that area a special status. This special status has been lost. The government cannot escape its responsibility to the slow-growth provinces such as Newfoundland and the other Atlantic provinces. The government has a responsibility to discharge in respect of the implementation of its special programs. It must be responsible to the regionally disadvantaged areas of the country.
These special programs can only be successful when the government recognizes that regional development must be approached on a regional basis. There must be regional application of this policy. What is good for the city of Montreal, the county of Glengarry or the southeastern area of Ontario is not necessarily good for Newfoundland, the Atlantic provinces, northern Ontario or the Gaspe region of Quebec.
It is a fact that unemployment in the Atlantic provinces is expected to reach 14 per cent of the work force this winter. What other area in Canada would tolerate such an astronomically high level of unemployment? This is the prospect we face in the Atlantic provinces. In Newfoundland and other parts of the Atlantic provinces, the rate of unemployment will actually exceed this figure. It may, as the hon. member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Lundrigan) suggests, go as high as 20 per cent. This government does not seem to realize that the structural causes of high unemployment in this region, such as
remoteness from major markets, an aging population, inadequate educational capacities and reduced capability of the work force, have been seriously aggravated by the government's anti-inflationary policies.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It is not good for the government to saddle a region with the high cost of its anti-inflation campaign and then, unsuccessfully, try to offset these costs with an inadequate regional incentives policy. I submit that the region must be provided with a new economic base. The Atlantic provinces must have a new economic base if they are to compete not only in terms of this program but under ordinary circumstances with the rest of Canada.
To quote the major recommendation of the fourth report of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, we must have a new economic base if we are to become a viable sector of the Canadian economy. RegretfuEy, I suggest to the House that we will not get that essential, new economic base under this program and consequently the program will fail, as it is failing now, to meet the needs of the Atlantic region. As I have said, what little advantage we had has been lost. We have lost the Uttle special status that we had. To realize this one has only to quote the recent reaction of APEC, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, in reference to the budget and to the government's proposal to designate Montreal and the southeastern area of Ontario as special area. The reaction was as follows:
If DREE wishes to counterbalance the designation of Montreal, Hull and Cornwall it has the power to do so by extending maximum grants to firms locating in the Atlantic region. Extending the ceiling is merely window-dressing.
Further in the same article there is this statement by the government of New Brunswick:
This will make it more difficult for us to attract new industrial firms, which will tend to locate in central Canada. Although Mr. Benson has indicated these are only for a limited time it will be difficult for Ottawa to resist local pressures to retain them.
By designating the city of Montreal and southeastern Ontario as special areas under the regional development incentives program, the government has in fact placed the Atlantic provinces at a further disadvantage which will become more painfully apparent this winter with the prospect of a record high rate of unemployment, the highest contemplated unemployment since the depression.
I listened today to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) refer to the need for a selective approach to areas of high unemployment. This is precisely the point we have been trying to make in the House since the government announced its program. I submit this is the point the government has failed to recognize in bringing down this policy. The government persists in taking a blanket approach to the problem, failing to recognize that this country is not one homogeneous unit but is, rather, comprised of five distinct areas each with a distinct economy. I submit this is a major weakness of the government's program to deal with regional economic development and is, regretfully, one which the Minister

December 8, 1970

of Finance (Mr. Benson) failed to recognize when he brought down his budget.
What is equally disturbing about the government's development policies is the arrogance that seem to personify the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The department takes an arrogant approach to the problems of regional disparity. We see it in the House in the minister's cavalier attitude in responding to questions on regional economic expansion. As a matter of fact, the attitude of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is such that we cannot seem to get an answer to a question in this House; he always seems to skate around the question.
One senses the same arrogance on the part of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, in the Standing Committee on Regional Development. The attitude of the minister, his deputy minister and the officials of the department toward the members of this Standing Committee of the House is such that they tell the members of the committee as little as possible. They completely fail to respond to questions. The minister and his officials evade questions and adopt a cavalier attitude, or one of non-cooperation, with the committee. The result is that this Standing Committee is one of the most ineffective committees of the House.
This committee should be in a position to help the government and the department in devising and implementing regional development incentives programs. This particular committee, of which I have the honour to be a member, has travelled throughout the country. It has visited many areas of western Canada, the Atlantic provinces and eastern Quebec where members of the committee had an opportunity to take a first-hand look at the existing programs for which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion assumed responsibility and see them at work. We had an opportunity to speak to the people in these areas.
However, the committee has failed to make a single recommendation to the House. As I say, it is the most ineffective committee of the House. I submit that a great deal of the blame for this situation rests with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and his deputy minister, because their attitude has created a situation of continuing frustration.
The arrogant attitude of this department, upon which so much dependence is placed by the government in this budget, is frightening. It is causing a great deal of concern because the government feels-certainly the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion feels-that in regional development programs it is preferable to proceed on the basis of trial and error rather than on the basis of listening to the elected representatives of the people and taking advice from the provinces and municipalities of this country. The minister, in a statement released today, explains the proposed amendments to the government's regional industrial incentives program as follows:
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We have had to learn some lessons by experiment. No doubt it will turn out that we have made a few mistakes.
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
Time does not permit me or my colleagues from disadvantaged areas of this country to catalogue those mistakes in the House because it is a substantial catalogue of trial and error. Why is it necessary for the government to proceed in this way? Why does the government not pay heed to the Standing Committee on Regional Development? Why does the government not pay attention to the members of this House who day after day direct questions to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion? In particular, why does the government not consult the provinces and the municipalities? Why does it persist in ignoring these essential sectors of government in respect of programs that can only be successful and effective so long as they have the complete trust and confidence of the provinces and municipalities? The government persists in its program of trial and error.
In the same statement the minister announced that in order to reduce the tremendous workload that is placed upon the shoulders of senior officials of his department in connection with the regional development incentives program, a special board would be established. I quote from the minister's statement as follows:
I therefore propose to establish a small board, consisting of my own senior officials plus representatives of the Department of Finance and of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, together with a few expert advisers from the private sector.
No reference whatsoever was made to the provinces and municipalities which have an essential part to play in any industrial incentives program and which have a very important role to play in any program of regional economic expansion. Why the government persists in this philosophy is beyond me. One can only conclude that this department, with its minister and deputy minister, its senior technocrats and bureaucrats, a department which every day grows in size and in organization, has an attitude of "we know best".
They have a condescending, cavalier attitude toward the provinces and municipalities of this country and to the House. They refuse to take advice in areas where programs they are implementing are essential to the local governments, municipal and provincial. Perhaps the attitude of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion can best be summed up by a comment that was made by an assistant deputy minister of the department at a conference on regional and rural economic adjustment which was held in Winnipeg from November 12 to 14, a conference sponsored by the Canadian Council on Rural Development and the Canadian Economic Association. He said that one of the reasons the performance of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was less than adequate was that DREE had to respond to political expediencies in their development program.
