subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the economic program of this government since it was elected in 1968 has achieved the paradoxical combination of a series of ad hoc decisions combined with a consistent and lunatic preoccupation with inflation. Even on the question of inflation itself the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has never been able to sort out whether he is dealing with the cost-push or demand-pull factors. We saw in his budget last spring all kinds of contradictory evidence on this point, and we saw the same kind of confused thinking in the budget which was brought before us last week.
The result of this kind of seriously and almost criminally directed effort has been that the growth rate of our economy has been reduced in effect to zero, if we consider the population growth and, not unrelated of course, we are about to achieve in Canada the highest number of unemployed in the history of our country. This has been the serious forecast by a number of competent economists regarding the trends which will reach their lamentable peak next February. This, I repeat, is a deplorable record for any government, and particularly deplorable in light of the expectations of hundreds of thousands of Canadians who thought they were electing a progressive Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Instead of dealing in a serious and meaningful way with the situation, instead of coming before Parliament and the people of Canada last Thursday with an imaginative, sound, serious program dedicated to achieving full employment and, not unrelated again, a sense of community in this country, we had the same kind of quick, unthought-out, contradictory proposals that have characterized the Minister of Finance since he assumed that position. The budget gives every indication of being concerned both with unemployment and inflation. The surtax is left on, yet all the rhetoric that is in the speech purports to reflect a concern for the unemployed position in which hundreds of thousands of Canadians find themselves. A trivial $250 million is to be given up by this government in its 115 per cent capital cost depreciation allowance program-a pitiful amount of money if we intend seriously to inject funds into the economy to do something about unemployment.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Firstly, the government proposes to grant an increase of $5 to a family man who is living on unemployment
insurance__a ridiculously low amount which would still
leave an unemployed man with a family at the poverty level. If you consider the budget seriously, these are the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
central recommendations. Instead of that, what was needed was a concerted attack on the present economic position of the country. We should have had an across the board tax cut for middle and low income families, and complete removal of taxation from family men and women with incomes up to $4,000 and single people with incomes up to $2,000.
Secondly, we should have had a major infusion of public capital into the economy. Thirdly, we should have had an indication from the government that it was going to establish a central economic planning board which would give serious priority to economic development. The amount of money that this party recommends, Mr. Speaker, is not the paltry $250 million that the minister is going to save on the 115 per cent capital cost depreciation allowance, but rather it is in the billions of dollars. That is what we need now, and we need it in a very serious way. It should not be spent in subsidizing private corporations but in the creation of Crown corporations and co-operatives on the one hand and, on the other, on encouraging public expenditure through municipal governments and agencies which already exist. I will return to that point.
It seems to me that this kind of spending through the public bodies and co-operatives on the one hand, spending on new enterprises and significant increases in expenditures at the municipal level on the other hand would achieve the desirable economic effect of injecting new cash into the economy and therefore would provide some increase-I do not want to exaggerate the possibilities^-in job opportunities.
The second important point to be made is that such money spent affects people living in our society on the basis of equality, and that is what the spending and the use of political power of democratic governments in our kind of society should be all about. Let me give specific examples of how this money could be spent in a way that would not just stimulate the economy but would benefit those who need it most. In respect of public housing, for example, approximately 2 million people are in need. In the city of Toronto alone there are 88,000 of these people. That is a rough calculation based on 22,000 families who right now need public housing. Yet the government is spending only 3.9 per cent of all its funds on public housing, which is less than 60 cents per capita. Spending in this area would have an important spin-off effect by encouraging full employment in all industries related to housing and it would provide housing to people who badly need it, many of whom are out of jobs.
Secondly, in terms of tax relief I have already said that tax cuts across the board are needed at the middle and low income levels, and we need the complete removal of income tax from single people earning up to $2,000 and from couples earning $4,000 or less. The other point I want to make with respect to tax reform, which should be introduced now and not postponed, is that the government, if it wants to redirect the economy, should get away from the ad hoc kind of decision-making that has gone on in Canada ever since World War II. It should take seriously the objective of stimulating and expanding
December 8, 1970

the public sector. It could have done this now by introducing special tax credits for those who want to purchase municipal and provincial bonds. This would be a significant reform.
It is in the area of municipal and provincial public spending that we can most readily affect those who have average and low incomes, because in the main the facilities provided by municipal and provincial governments are provided to citizens on the basis of equality. It makes no difference whether a child is a member of a rich or a poor family in terms of whether that child benefits from public schools, public universities, public parks, public swimming pools, or what have you.
It is just this kind of shifting of priorities that we need in our economy if we are to take simultaneously and seriously the democratic objective of equality and the economic objective of stable employment. But no such indication has come from the government, certainly not in this budget and certainly not in the white paper on tax reform.
The hundreds of thousands now unemployed, the fishermen in Newfoundland, the auto workers in my constituency who were unemployed in their thousands before the strike which is currently taking place and will likely remain so after it has been settled, the unemployed cab drivers in this city-in short, the unemployed throughout the country-need their unemployment insurance benefits increased and increased immediately. Those benefits need to be increased much more than the paltry $5 which the government offers for the family man. The very minimum we need, and need now, is the kind of proposal in the white paper on unemployment insurance. There is no reason why an unemployed man in this country should not receive at least two-thirds of his income during periods of unemployment. He does not create that unemployment. It is created by the economic policies of government, whether it be federal or provincial, and neither he nor his family should have to suffer the consequences.
In terms of public spending, the government could have shown a little imagination. For example, it could have decided to develop winter parks in the way that many of the provinces have developed summer parks. We could have taken our national parks and installed several ski-tows in each of them at a cost of $50,000 or $60,000 per tow. That would provide a minimal kind of employment initially, but at the same time it would provide a real opportunity for skiing Canadians who happen to earn less than the $15,500, which is the average income of skiers in this country, to use such facilities. We could provide a meaningful and exciting winter parks program for the people of this northern country instead of leaving our recreational facilities in the winter available primarily for the rich.
Also, at the time of the budget announcement the government could have decided that it would no longer leave to corporations the unfettered right to open and close factories. We could have taken away from Duplate Canada Limited and the Dunlop Corporation of Canada Limited the right unilaterally to throw hundreds of workers out of work even though the men and women
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent might have been in those jobs for up to 35 years. It is not merely the human right to have some say about your job that is at stake here-and that is an important right-but also at stake is the unfettered right of corporations to make these investment decisions. Only by getting at that kind of control which currently remains with our corporate sector can we effectively develop an economy based upon the principle and the goal of full employment.
Much of the fooling around with the system, the special tax allowances and so on, that the government seems to admire so much is totally and completely wasted. What is needed instead is a serious effort by the government to have some say in these investment decisions. But, Mr. Speaker, that would mean effectively taking on the corporate directors in this society, and no Liberal government in the past-and certainly not this Liberal government-has shown the slightest indication of willingness to take this kind of action.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about "Tiger" Basford? He takes them on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member who preceded me talked convincingly about the inadequacy of the regional development program. He did not mention that over 60 per cent of the funds which have gone into that program since the election of this government have gone into foreign-owned industries. We are perpetuating, in underdeveloped parts of Canada, the economic sickness which is reflected in the developed regions. Our party has argued that this kind of financial assistance to foreign-owned firms should cease immediately. We are not saying that no foreign capital should come in; that should be made clear. However, we are insisting that when it comes in, it ought to come in on the basis of a minority shareholder.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Instead of relying overwhelmingly, as we now do in regional development programs, on foreign-owned firms which will distort the priorities of our economy and which will contribute to the boom and bust cycle, we should be encouraging a combination of mixed capital development projects, using federal funds and private Canadian capital as well as private foreign capital. This method has been used in Turkey, in Sweden and in Japan. It has been used so often that one would think even Liberals had learned about it.
In addition, we should use in many cases public capital exclusively for investment in development. In some cases we ought to create entirely new enterprises, and in some cases we ought to buy up existing enterprises, especially those in the natural resource sectors. We have some $4 billion now in the reserve fund. A good part of that money will not be needed if we maintain a floating exchange rate. I do not see why a good part of this money should not be used to gain control, for example, of the oil and gas industry in this country. This would stop the export of the profits of that industry. Also-and this is at least of equal importance-it is a modern industry

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent in this society and in the modern world economy. It has real potential for growth.
By gaining control of that kind of industry we would begin to control the research and development that is related to its ownership. We could begin to develop in Canada, for example, many of the new products that are associated with the petrochemical industry in its operations all over the world. These products are being currently developed outside our borders because the industry is foreign-owned. This kind of imaginative step, if taken, would not have provided remarkable, short-run improvements in our unemployment situation. It would have provided some new jobs; there is no doubt about that. However, such a step would have indicated that this government is interested in bringing about a structural change in the economy and that it is providing for real, economic growth in the future. In the budget speech there is not the slightest hint that the government intends to move in this direction.
Finally, what is needed is a federal economics planning board. This board ought to be concerned about all the areas I have mentioned. It ought to encourage the development-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ought to do this-of equivalent planning boards in all provinces so as to co-ordinate the investment priorities as between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities of this country. Such a step would require, of course, the federal government and provincial governments to assume a number of the powers currently held by corporations, especially the exclusive power to determine their investment priorities. That is the kind of deliberate action that is required, and only that kind of action will begin to have, in the long run, a significant effect on our economy.
What would be the net effect of the proposals that I have made? Some are specific and some are rather general in nature. It would be irresponsible of me to suggest that in the short run thousands of new jobs would be created. That would not be the case. There would be many new jobs created if we started to put money into housing, streets, schools and new, publicly-owned enterprises; but it would take time for the effects to be really felt. Probably they would not be felt until next spring, at best.
In addition to the short-run economic effects, however, there would be other benefits. The people of this country would sense that we have a government that is concerned about equality for all the people, about equality of condition for all the people of this nation. If in the short-run such action is unable to bring about 100 per cent employment for our people, and if it is unable to bring about a purely egalitarian situation, it would enable us to regain control of our economy over a period of time. It would be seen that the government fully intends to use democratic power in the economic sector of our society to bring about the kind of full democracy that is surely desired by all. Such action, in short, would give the people of our country who are now living in a condition of unemployment without power and lacking in dignity, a real basis and legitimate foundation for believing there is hope for the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like in opening my remarks to extend my felicitations to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) who made his maiden speech a little earlier in this debate. He has succeeded a man who was well known to many of us and dearly beloved. In following in the footsteps that George Muir trod in this House, I wish him well. The hon. member expressed some concern that many of us in the House think of the west as beginning at Calgary, Edmonton or Vancouver rather than at Lisgar. May I assure him that when he has been here a little longer he will find that many members think the west begins at Oakville or Hamilton.
In the debate this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) joined in the general clamour for a tax reduction and increased social programs, while all the time complaining about the government's increasing pressure on the capital markets as a result of the deficit proposed in the budget that we are considering. As nimble as he is, the Leader of the Opposition will have difficulty keeping all those dumbbells in the air at one time. There are some contradictions that we must face in terms of simple arithmetic if not sophisticated economics.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The Leader of the Opposition has suggested that monetary and fiscal policies alone cannot do the job of curing inflation; that we must supplement these with an incomes policy, although he says this has not worked satisfactorily anywhere. If left with monetary and fiscal policies as the main weapons against inflation, how would he use them? How would he maintain the full employment that he advocates and still bring the long, inflationary spiral under control? This, Mr. Speaker, is an aim that no country, regardless of the degree of intervention the government has taken in the private sector, has succeeded in achieving.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) earlier today advocated large expenditures in terms of schools, hospitals and like items of social developments, as well as increased financial assistance to the aged, disabled and unemployed. He also advocated a tax reduction for those in the low income group. He at least had the decency not to criticize the government for pressure on capital markets in view of the program that he was advocating. However, he was concerned about what he alleged were the stop-go programs that this government had adopted. I asked him to recall the problems that the Labour government in Britain faced when it pledged to end its stop-go policies. They were obliged to follow stop-only policies in order to prevent inflation caused by the wage demands of the unions that supported them. That party is no longer in power.
The reaction of the opposition parties to this budget provides the clearest indication so far as to how bankrupt they are in policies and programs for promoting strong, stable, long-term growth in our economy. The Conservatives and New Democrats have engaged in a contest to outbid each other in extravagance in their proposals for creating a massive government deficit through mammoth
[Mr. Broadbent.1
December 8, 1970

increases in spending and a major reduction in government revenue through tax cuts. There would be economic disaster for Canada if the government were to adopt their proposals, or if through some misfortune they had the opportunity to implement them.
With regard to inflation, opposition parties have over a number of years belaboured the government when prices have risen, acknowledging that inflation is a critical national problem. Yet they have opposed virtually all measures adopted by the government to deal with this problem, measures of a kind which the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development and the International Monetary Fund recently urged other governments to follow.
I quote as follows a number of recommendations of the OECD for the coming 12 to 18-month period for countries facing inflation:
AH member countries should aim to restore at least the degree of price stability associated in the past with sustainable levels of employment and economic growth. To this end, cautious demand management policies are required. Excess demand should be eliminated and governments should be prepared, where necessary, to accept temporarily some slack in the use of resources until there are signs that better price stability has been achieved.
I believe Canada has achieved that position. Other nations have yet to achieve it. I continue quoting:
In cases where unemployment is rising towards unacceptable levels, attention should be directed to the possibility of selective action directed to areas of high unemployment, rather than indiscriminate increases in public expenditure or general tax cuts. Within the framework of appropriate over-all fiscal restraint, expenditure on government-sponsored manpower training and relocation programs should be increased as much and as quickly as is possible.
That is precisely what this budget is all about. This budget is a series of measures of selective action directed toward areas of high unemployment. It is not indiscriminate increases in public expenditure or general tax cuts. The third recommendation of the OECD made last month is as follows:
Despite the difficulties, the search for effective price-incomes policies should not be abandoned; but this should be regarded as a long-haul operation unlikely to yield miracles.
I think it has been proved to our satisfaction that this has not yielded miracles in Canada. The government is pursuing these policies in an attempt to achieve all that it can within the limits of our Constitution. We have every confidence that in the long haul we will indeed achieve these objectives.
Experience has shown that the present inflationary round that Canada, as well as other nations, has had the misfortune of having is one of the most serious and intractable ever to develop in the post-war period. What solutions have the Progressive Conservatives advanced to halt this inflationary spiral? They have urged the adoption of voluntary restraint guidelines. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition stated that the government adopted these guidelines a year or two too early and that now is the time to be pushing them. That is regrettable.
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
The government in fact did this long ago through the establishment of the Prices and Incomes Commission. The Conservatives also advocate the abolition of the sales tax on building materials. Is it possible to imagine that so major and critical a problem could be overcome by such a bromide?
The exercise of responsible restraint by all sectors of the economy is desirable and necessary. However, the OECD, the International Monetary Fund and the Economic Council of Canada have all underlined the fact that such restraint can only be a supplement to other measures adopted by governments to put out inflationary fires. In fact, Conservative proposals for dealing with inflation are so devoid of substance as to be ludicrous.
The Conservatives have charged that the government has done too little, too late, to deal with the problem of unemployment. They now urge mammoth increases in spending and mammoth tax cuts. This is diametrically opposed to the course they proposed some months ago. What was the position of the Conservative party earlier this year? When estimates for the current year were tabled in this House in Feburary, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the party's financial critic, strongly criticized the projected increase of $900 million. He said:
When we consider that in 1963-64 the total estimates or total expenditures of the government were just over $6.4 billion, we can see that the series of Liberal administrations has more than doubled government expenditures at the federal level. We have complained from time to time that this government follows the practice of taxing up to expenditures. It is for this reason that we are facing continuous surcharges or additional taxes.
In the budget debate on March 12, the hon. member for Edmonton West again complained about the projected $900 million increase in benefits and said:
That is not controlling expenditures. If there were to be control, if there were to be a real fight against inflation by fiscal measures, we would be taxing to defeat inflation, not merely to catch up with the bills that are coming into the government.
Speaking in this House during the Throne Speech debate in October, the hon. member for Edmonton West dismissed as insufficient the series of measures adopted by the government since the last budget. He contended that a "much more massive injection must be furnished by the government". In this House, on November 12, the Leader of the Opposition urged major increases in spending, echoing the New Democratic Party's proposal for calling a federal-provincial conference to discuss development of a public works program, in addition to substantial spending in other areas.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The Leader of the Opposition also proposed tax cuts on the same occasion suggesting it would be "very interesting" to see whether this would work to counter inflation. While his proposal was lacking in clarity, he appeared to suggest that the surtax should be allowed to expire and income taxes reduced a further 6 per cent. This, presumably, was in addition to the abolition of the sales tax on

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
building materials. The cost of these tax cuts would be as follows. The elimination of the 3 per cent surtax would cost $240 million, the reduction of personal income tax by 6 per cent would cost the treasury $310 million and the cost to the provinces as a result of the same cut could be $135 million.
In addition, eliminating the sales tax on building materials would cost $360 million, and if the Leader of the Opposition intended that his proposed 6 per cent income tax cut should extend to corporations as well as to individuals, the treasury would lose a further $118 million. In other words, the total cost of these suggestions to the treasury, if implemented, would be $1,163 million, or $1.04 billion if the 6 per cent reduction in corporation tax is excluded.
The New Democratic Party has recognized that inflation is a serious problem and has acknowledged the need to employ fiscal and monetary restraints to help overcome it. Nevertheless, they have continued to urge a massive expansion within the existing framework of fiscal and monetary policy which would have the very opposite effect. They have suggested that inflation could be overcome by the imposition of controls over prices and incomes, although recently they have been shifting away from this position.

speechtext: Hurrah!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For his part, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) proposed to increase the exemption for single people to $2,000 and the exemption for married people to $4,000. This would cost the federal treasury around $1,750 million and the provinces a further $500 million, based on 1969 tax receipts. He also suggested, though he was far from specific about it, that tax relief should be provided for those in the middle-income bracket. This concern for people in the middle-income bracket on the part of the hon. member for Waterloo is novel, especially to hon. members who had the pleasure of sitting with him on the finance committee during the past year while the white paper on tax reform was under consideration. As I say, the hon. member did not tell us what reduction or rate changes he had in mind for people in the middle-income group, so it is impossible to assess the cost which would be involved in his proposal.
It is difficult to know where one stands in connection with this general recommendation to alleviate the plight of people in the middle-income group. In addition, we lack a definition of "middle-income group", something which the hon. member was most assiduous in trying to dig out when various witnesses appeared before the finance committee last year. Perhaps he will take an opportunity to make his views on this matter clear at an early date. The hon. member also suggested that the budget was economic lunacy. This would have to be taken as something of an expert opinion and contrasted with the position advocated by the NDP, which would truly be the action of a government gone mad.
The government has proposed a series of measures since the last budget, the cumulative effect of which has been strongly expansionist. The government could have chosen to cut taxes instead of directing spending into areas of slow growth and high unemployment. The greatest advantage would then have gone to areas of the country already prosperous and with considerably lower unemployment. The benefit to slow-growth areas would have trickled down only partially and slowly. The approach of the government is in line with the course advocated by the OECD in its report last month to ministers on the Economic Policy Committee, namely:
In cases where unemployment is rising toward unacceptable levels, attention should be directed to the possibility of selective action directed to areas of high unemployment, rather than indiscriminate increases in public expenditures or general tax cuts.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) made clear in the budget, there are real limits as to how far the government can go in adopting expansionary policies without creating an excessive risk of new inflation. One of the lessons learned from the sixties was that it is danger-

December 8, 1970

ous to expand the money supply in order to finance massive government deficits, setting the stage for a new round of inflation. Yet this is the advice the opposition gives us. This point, again, is underlined by the Economic Council in its recent report, "Performance and Potential".
Monetary policy (together with fiscal policy with which it is closely interrelated) should evolve in a way that seeks to avoid large destabilizing swings in the growth of the money supply. There are long lags between changes in policy and their effects on the economy.. .For the creation of a stable environment for growth, we therefore consider it essential that the growth of the money supply over the longer term should be approximately in line with the underlying growth rate of potential output, with smaller swings around the rate of increase in potential output than have characterized past policy.

The hon. member for Edmonton West took specific issue with the proposal in the budget concerning investment incentive credit. He said it would have only a slow effect in spurring capital investment due to the length of time required to make expenditures. Indications of investment spending intentions show that there is a large carryover of capital programs already planned by the big-business sector and ready to roll once conditions are considered appropriate. These were deferred during 1970 because of market conditions and the expectation of a fall in interest rates. The effect of the increased capital cost allowance will be similar to that of a reduction in borrowing costs and it is expected it will produce a quick reaction.
We have been treated to a very similar response on the part of both the official opposition and the New Democratic Party. Their leaders are anxious to spend more money and to take in less by way of taxes, to provide greater incentives, increased social programs, increased expenditure on public works, extended and expanded assistance programs, all on the basis of decreased revenues and, evidently, without significant borrowing so as not to exert inflationary pressure on capital markets. This game of leapfrog, this game of bribing taxpayers with their own money, is far more typical of an era of minority government, of insecure government with the opposition tasting the prospect of office. Perhaps what we are looking at today is the phenomenon of minority opposition-an insecure official opposition and a New Democratic Party tasting office and hoping to convert ineffective opposition into official opposition.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Fronlenac-Lennox and Adding-Ion):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was preparing my notes for today's debate I made a special effort to avoid areas of sensitivity for the present government. I did this out of a sense of compassion. I really do not want to embarrass the government or any of the puppets of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Every day that passes must surely be embarrassment enough in itself when you consider that we end up with more problems and fewer solutions than we had the day before.
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
Canada is plagued by many corporate ills at the present time. Chief and most injurious of these to her progress are the following. First, a Liberal government and a Liberal syndrome of permissiveness, contempt of the law, corruption and waste in administration, and even contempt of Parliament. The latest example of this was the government's efforts to downgrade and make less effective the Auditor General's department. Second, there is a mounting national debt too great for the taxpayers to handle. Cost of servicing this debt alone amounts to $1,704 million a year. I obtained that figure this evening and I believe it is correct.
Third, we have an overstaffed and economically unproductive, and in some respects empirical civil service, in number and cost out of proportion to the needs of the country. Fourth, we have an extravagant and wasteful annual budget running currently at $14 billion, the source of which is inexorably being levied from fewer and fewer taxpayers in the middle-income class who at the same time are being deprived of family benefits and allowances.
However, there is nothing that one can say about the way this country is being run without causing great embarrassment to that army of experts on the front benches opposite. They must surely be experts, because this government and the Cabinet that is composed mainly of former civil servants can turn out more white papers on more subjects than any other government has since this country was founded. But apparently the brand of expertise available to the Prime Minister is not equal to the problems that beg solution. We on this side of the House, indeed millions of Canadians from coast to coast, would gladly trade all of this questionable expertise across the floor of this House for just a little bit of applied common sense.
The budget that the government tabled last week is a good case in point, Mr. Speaker. Our jovial finance minister has stated that there are solutions in the budget to a wide range of serious problems, though so far no one has been able to point them out. One day last week the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) suggested that the finance minister was the Charlie McCarthy of the chartered banks. I have to disagree with that analogy, though I can certainly go along with the sense of the hon. member's statement. Charlie McCarthy had real talent. McCarthy could fool all of the people all of the time and make them like it. Our finance minister cannot fool any of the people any of the time, especially from now on, and he certainly cannot make anybody like what he is doing. This budget is not recognized as such by many people. Indeed, one Liberal today called it simply a financial report.
Whatever the present government tackles, we end up with another little island of chaos. The fear is spreading across the country that these islands will all come together and we will have general chaos. However, Canada is resilient, and so are Canadians, and I firmly believe that the next general election will remove this treat to our economy and way of life.

December 8, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
There is one thing that can be said to the credit of the present government, and that is that it is consistent. This government can be counted upon to do some things as regularly as clockwork, and for this it deserves full marks. Here again I point to the budget that we are presently debating, in which the finance minister showed consistency. He tabled a budget when there was no demonstrable need for a budget at this time. That is why my Liberal friend called it a report. There was and is enabling legislation whereby, the minister could have accomplished any of the measures proposed in this budget that might be considered worth while. Yet apparently the minister was unaware that he had that authority, and so once again he was consistent. This is a nothing budget, and we have seen a succession of nothing budgets from the present government. I did not want to miss this opportunity to give credit where credit is due.
There is another area wherein this government is consistent and shows evidence of real finesse. The present administration has to be considered the all-time champion in the game of sloganeering. First we had the just society. This was laughed out of existence, and personally I was disappointed. I very much wanted the Prime Minister to create this just society because there were many adjustments to be made to our system. I wanted him to elevate all of us to a little higher plane of existence. I hated to see that one go by the board.
Then in the Speech from the Throne we were told that we were on the threshold of greatness. I really got caught up on this one. The idea that somehow we could achieve greatness in spite of the bungling and ineptitude displayed on the other side of the House was an intriguing one. However, my hopes were dashed again when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) exposed that particular slogan. Our leader reasoned that the Prime Minister was referring to the Conservative victory at the next general election, so I find I will have to wait a couple of years before 1 can achieve a share of this greatness.
However, Mr. Speaker, I really do not mind the wait, because every day that passes finds more and more Canadians wondering how this government, with one of the best mandates in the history of Canada and with the largest budget in our history, totalling $14 billion, manages to provide so little for Canadians. But this is the day of reckoning, the day that the government hoped would not come. The government has called the tune and has danced; it will now have to pay the fiddler. But that is not all. The slogans are still coming and they get better all the time. We now have the Prime Minister caricatured as Robin Hood riding through the country robbing the rich and giving to the poor. Robin Hood rides straight out of the finance minister's budget, and this is very fitting. If there were not so many people across this country in dire need at the present time, this would be the funniest slogan to come out of the government's slogan department in a long time. But it is not funny, Mr. Speaker.
There always seems to be a key phrase in every document that this government tables that points straight to
the fallacies that are inherent in all of them, and this so-called budget is no exception. We are told that there are many rich people in Canada. In fact, everyone in this country who makes $10,000 or more must now consider himself to be rich. He must wait for Robin Hood to pay him a visit and then he must pay up-again, again and again. There appears to be no end to the price one must pay in this country for the "sin" of being self-supporting. There is no end to the penalties one must pay in this country for the "sin" of being enterprising and for displaying initiative.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
A few days ago I asked a question in this House about the government's policy of permissiveness with regard to allowing Cuban embassy and consular officials to openly support extremist and revolutionary groups and activities in Canada. This question may be found at page 1716 of Hansard for December 3. I found out shortly afterwards that there is general concern throughout our country over this apparent disregard for threats against our social and political systems. However, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) answered in general terms about the present regulations being sufficient to screen persons coming to Canada to visit or to settle. He avoided the purport of my question and he had good reason to avoid it. The relations that exist between the revolutionary Cubans and other elements in our country made it possible for the government to get the kidnappers of James Cross out of the country in a matter of hours. It appears that all of them will be allowed to keep their Canadian citizenship. This attitude bears looking into.
There is evidence that this government is exhibiting a lack of leadership and concern with regard to safeguarding Canadian life, property and traditionally Canadian institutions. In addition to the unrestrained efforts of Cuban diplomatic officials to finance and train terrorists in Canada, the present government flatly refuses to use the powers inherent in the Immigration Act to prevent people like Abbie Hoffman, William Kunstler, the Black Panthers and others coming to Canada to spread their poison and treason throughout our country. In a recent issue of the Globe and Mail, MacKenzie Porter quoted from a speech by Dr. Roger Gaudry, rector of the University of Montreal. I think this quotation should be recorded in Hansard. It reads as follows:
Ideological chapels have grown up in our universities so that a young professor who wished in certain cases to defend the position of a government that was not left wing, or to defend a position that is not left wing, would be quickly put down by his colleagues.
Dr. Gaudry in his speech was emphasizing the great danger we face today from the direction of our universities, the very institutions we should look to for intellectual defence of our system, particularly because of the influence of left wing faculty members. These people, these leftists, are getting a lot of direct and indirect support. The taxpayers' money is going to the Company

December 8, 1970

of Young Canadians in spite of clear evidence before committee hearings that CYC personnel in Quebec have been giving support to the FLQ. When the committee hearings were in progress in the fall of 1969, the government said the FLQ was not a threat and that there was no reason to inhibit the CYC on those grounds. Scarcely one year later the Prime Minister implied that the FLQ was about to take over the province of Quebec and possibly the ent're country, and it was necessary therefore to invoke the War Measures Act.
I pointed out earlier that the present government is often inconsistent, at least in certain areas. 1 should also point out that it can also be inconsistent in other areas, and it is the government's inconsistencies that pose the greatest danger. I could also mention the thousands of draft-dodgers, deserters and other weirdos the government encourages to come to Canada to swell the ranks of revolutionaries and also the ranks of the unemployed. But such warnings would only fall on deaf ears, ears that will not hear, eyes that will not see and minds that will not reason. What we are witnessing is a tragic comedy; the tragedy of dissipating God-given resources, both natural and human, and the plundering of willing minds.
But all is not lost. We have the blundering of the government to lighten our hours in the conviction that we have only a couple of years to go before the voters indicate that blundering has proven too costly to tolerate and that the Liberal syndrome and the fallacy and myth of "Trudeaucratic" charisma does nothing for Canada's ills.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes remaining before the vote, I should like to make a few remarks on the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he brought down the budget on December 3rd.
It will be remembered that last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asked the Canadians to tighten up their belts in the fight against inflation, and that in a subsequent speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) told them: Work more, increase productivity, to fight inflation. The Prime Minister said: Do without; while the Minister of Finance said: Work hard.
I remember that, at the time, we had said that the means suggested to overcome inflation would probably result in increased unemployment in Canada, mostly in underdevelopped areas. Our predictions unfortunately came true since, according to the December 1st edition of La Presse, more than 10,000 Quebecers lost their job in 1970.
For instance, the Canadian Marconi Company has fired 800 people since the beginning of the year and expects to fire 700 more before the end of the year.
At Les Industries Valcartier in the Quebec City area, a subsidiary of the General Investment Corporation, the layoff of 500 to 1,000 workers is anticipated before the end of the year.
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
The Northern Electric Company has dismissed 200 of its employees and expects further layoffs.
On the other hand, the United Aircraft Company which had a staff of more than 5,400 employees had only 4,500 as of December 1.
The same applies to the Wabasso Company in Drum-mondville which has apparently dismissed from 500 to 600 employees during 1970.
Going down the list, we would note that dismissals affect 500, 600 or 1,000 employees at the same time.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance stated that most economic indicators showed improving trends in the Canadian economy, an increase in employment, a decrease in unemployment and a recovery in the production of goods and services.
Mr. Speaker, if this inquiry had been made more seriously in sectors others than the manufacturing or industrial sector, we would have indeed found out that the number of unemployed has risen significantly, because a great number of farmers including those involved in the production of industrial milk have ceased producing because of the dairy policy of this government which does not allow the smaller farmers to operate their business and stay on the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, if we give the situation a closer look, we realize that a certain number of young people who are just out of school will soon be on the labour market. Although they have no particular experience, they no longer belong to the student population. Therefore they cannot claim any unemployment insurance benefits or obtain any other form of aid to the unemployed.
Thousands of these students are willing to work, but their names are not on the list of the 10,000 people who have lost their jobs in Quebec. They represent however a number of workers important enough to deserve consideration.
The policy outlined by the government in the budget speech will not be enough, in my opinion, to stop inflation and reduce unemployment, especially in eastern Quebec where conditions are alarmingly bad.
For instance, at Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere, a snowmobile factory employing a certain number of workers has laid off over 250 of them in the last two weeks. Those workers will be unemployed for an indefinite period of time, because the factory owners are unable to sell their snowmobiles fast enough. Warehouses are full and that was the reason for the employer's decision.
In order to get the economy moving again, the government should have proposed a tax reduction and primarily the removal of the tax on building materials. In the field of construction, the situation is none too good as this tax on building materials contributes to the increased cost of houses, and this coupled with the high rate of interest, prevents promoters from building houses and renting them at prices suitable to workers.
Mr. Speaker, I see you looking at the clock. I must resume my seat as it is 9.45 and the House has to vote on the sub-amendment.
